en: The Scripture on the Samādhi Asked by the Dragon King Sāgara, Spoken by the Buddha.
Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Lokakṣema of the Yuezhi during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha together with sixty thousand bhikṣus and seventy-three thousand bodhisattvas.

Each of these honored ones had come from buddha-fields in the ten directions; they had all attained the dhāraṇī-dharmas, their desires were without obstruction, and they had achieved perfection through practicing much patience and a sense of shame regarding the thoughts of their minds.
His mind is like a vajra, such that nothing can sever it; he desires to fully perfect all the practices and all the qualities of the Buddhas.
The aspirations of his will are most sublime, and his mind never departs from the bodhicitta, causing others to do likewise.
They practice giving with a subdued mind free from distraction, cherishing others without any sense of loss;
they adorn themselves with the discipline of pure precepts, embellishing body, speech, and mind;
their patience is gentle and supple—this is indeed power, this is indeed the armor of resolve (*saṃnāha*).
Recalling the deeds performed throughout hundreds of thousands of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he was diligent and never indolent;
in meditation, he devoted himself to samādhi and samāpatti, his mind knowing the thoughts of others, thereby finding delight within himself;
as for the merit of his wisdom, there was nothing he did not understand.
His mind is like Mount Sumeru, beyond all comparison;
his mind is like earth, water, fire, and wind—neither loving nor hating, always possessing a heart of compassion.
The radiance of his body is unimpeded.
His compassionate practice brings forth a heart of sorrow for all people.
Having attained equanimity through the Dharma, he finds joy therein; as a protector, he does not fall into a single path.
Whether there is gain or loss, praise or blame, fame or insignificance, suffering or pleasure—transcending all such worldly phenomena, he does not regard any assembly as a true assembly.
He repels all non-Buddhists and subdues the hosts of Māras.
Such a person is difficult to encounter, appearing only once in a great while like the udumbara flower.
He acts as a benefactor for all people who have no patron; therefore he is called "Thick" (thou). This "Thickness" leads one to the ultimate state of Nirvāṇa.
Having already attained the supreme saṃnāha-saṃnaddha, their profound Dharma is as fierce as a lion;
they have been sealed with the seal of the Tathāgata, and having received their prediction, they are without any obstruction.
Their actions accord with their words; having realized the Dharma, they are discerning.
Their radiance outshines the sun and moon, and there is none throughout the ten directions who has not heard their name.
All Buddhas protect and deliver them, ensuring they do not depart from the Dharma; all uphold the profound Dharma so that it does not perish, and they ensure the Three Jewels are never severed.
The merit of that mind pervades countless lands; that mind is pure and clean, and as it practices its course through coming and going, it reaches the presence of the Buddha without any loss.

Constantly teaching and guiding all people, having already entered the *prajñāpāramitā* and *upāyakauśalya*, they then follow the inclinations of each person’s mind to illuminate them with the Dharma, causing each to obtain what they seek.
Knowing the various characteristics of people and their inclinations and preferences, he does not fail to accord with their intentions;
thus, he manifests the virtue of a King of Physicians to treat old age, sickness, and death.
Having made offerings to countless Buddhas of the past, his merit has brought about the primary marks and secondary signs.
He has transcended the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; all phenomena are non-existent, like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, a reflection in water, or an echo in the mountains.
He fully knows all sounds and voices, penetrating into all phenomena and being able to answer each one.
Having already attained mastery over all that is desired, he understands the matters of the Way through wisdom.

Having drawn somewhat near to the Ten Powers of the Honored One, their physical eyes, wisdom eyes, path eyes, dharma eyes, and Buddha eyes have transcended all darkness; they have fully entered into all meritorious practices and clearly understand the treasury of the bodhisattvas.

Upon hearing this Dharma, they no longer regress and immediately attain the Samādhi of the Seal of Characteristics, the Samādhi of Vajra Practice, the Samādhi of That Dharma Abiding in All Actions, the Samādhi of Holding Jewel Radiance, and the Samādhi of Not Forsaking Any Being.
Having fully realized the samādhi that knows all minds, one attains the wisdom of a Buddha.
Just as the deeds of a Buddha serve as the foundation for all actions, one has already become fully endowed with all the marks of excellence.

Śrī and forty-nine others—such bodhisattvas as these, numbering seventy-three thousand, were present in the assembly.

From throughout the trichiliocosm, Śakras, Brahmās, and world-protectors; from each of the noble lords among the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—all came to the assembly, desiring to hear the sūtra spoken by the Buddha.
The Bodhisattva Vimukta rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and praised the Buddha’s teaching, saying:
“The worldly cannot equal the brilliance of the Way; it serves as the foundation for the world and has already transcended all darkness. I now take refuge in the one who delivers the world.”

"By means of generosity, dhāraṇī, and the ten powers, you have already subdued your own mind and transformed others; thus, you are the one who delivers all beings such that there is none who does not serve you. Now I take refuge in you, the peerless one within the triple world—this is the first."

"Because his marks bring benefit to all without exception, his radiance is doubly red like gold, his voice is harmonious and balanced, and his appearance is exceedingly sublime such that none can equal it; we now take refuge in him who is served by all. (Three) The third [refuge]: "Because his marks bring benefit to all without exception, his radiance is doubly red like gold, his voice is harmonious and balanced, and his appearance is exceedingly sublime such that none can equal it; we now take refuge in him who is served by all. (Three)

"Having crossed over, he delivers others; having subdued all non-Buddhists, his wisdom is most sublime, standing at the pinnacle of all the wise, such that none can shake or move him. He fully knows all modes of conduct, and his merit is most sublime. Now we take refuge in the Great Compassion that is infinite. (4)
"Regarding all desires, he finds nothing to be grasped among them; having already exhausted all Māras, none can withstand him.

His pure precepts are entirely without instability; among all the devas, he is the God of Gods. His mind no longer clings to anything; now I take refuge in him, the one whom none can withstand—this is the fifth."
"Those who hear of his virtue do not fail to rejoice;
his physical form is like a precious jewel, and there are none who, upon seeing him, do not love and delight in him.
Having practiced generosity, he is free from lust, anger, and delusion. Now we take refuge in his virtue, which, like heaven, covers all without exception. (6)

Because the Four Truths transcend the four gates, those who lack eyes all obtain the power of vision; the Dharma you preach is boundless and bottomless, serving as the foundation for the conduct of all beings throughout the three periods of time. Now I take refuge in your feet, which bear the seven wheels.
"His person is served and honored by all the devas and all people; whether male or female, all may rely upon him.
The various māras dare not oppose him; this is the eighth quality by which he is uniquely venerated in the heavens above and the world below."
"By means of the many truths and righteous laws, he sustains all things; his mind is equal in compassion, reaching everywhere without exception.
He acts as a guide for all, and his Dharma abides in equanimity. Now I take refuge in him whose virtue is unsurpassed—this is the ninth."
“His voice is supple and pure; there is no one who hears it whose heart is not gladdened.
His sound is like that of Brahmā, reaching everywhere.
It is fully endowed with all qualities of sound. Now we take refuge in the Honored One, the Tenth Truth.”
"Having already transcended emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, his wisdom is profoundly deep and ungraspable.
His faculties have entered into manifold liberations; this is his merit. I now take refuge in him who has attained liberation—eleven times."

"Having fully understood the merit arising from causes and conditions, his vision is neither internal nor external; because it is equal, his knowledge and speech differ from conventional fabrication. Now he has taken refuge and transcended all twelve objects of perception."
"Furthermore, they come from nowhere and go nowhere; one perceives all phenomena as entirely liberated, like a phantom or a mirage. This is the thirteenth merit of taking refuge in the Dharma."
That which is produced has no locus; production and non-production are both non-arising.
That which exists has already ceased, and there is no time of its exhaustion.
Its abiding is according to the Dharma, just as the Tathāgata enters the fourteen [unanswerable questions].
"It is exactly as you have said: if a dharma is such that it is like the Tathāgata, being without movement or change;
if its merit is like a great mountain and its body is like adamant, then we now take refuge in this peace which is like a mountain—this is the fifteenth."
"His body, mind, and intellect are perfectly balanced; his name circulates through the three periods of time, and there is no one who has not heard it.
He is able to answer every question posed to him, yet he does so with such ease that he never tires of speaking."
“I wish to ask sixteen questions; having praised the Buddha, if you would deign to speak, I shall ask them.
The Buddha said, “Ask whatever you wish.”
Ti-wu-li said: "What is meant by a bodhisattva adorning the body through the mastery of teaching the Dharma (1)?
What is meant by a bodhisattva swiftly entering into all profound dharmas without exception (2)?"
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the three types of mental states of all people?
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s transformation according to what others delight in?
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s entry through the activities of the mind?
What are the six ways in which a bodhisattva knows that there is purposeful action through causes and conditions?
What are the seven ways in which a bodhisattva practices giving as an adornment for upholding ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the state of Brahmā?
(8) What is meant by a bodhisattva whose wisdom is most exalted?
(9) What is meant by a bodhisattva who always attains victory? (10)
What is meant by the eleventh [point]: how a bodhisattva attains deliverance from this?
What is meant by the twelfth: how a bodhisattva manifests the Dharma among śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all people, yet does not enter into their midst?
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s remaining apart from birth and death without entering parinirvāṇa?
(13) What is meant by the bodhisattva’s knowing that all realms of sentient beings are not separate from the dharmakāya? (14)
What is meant by the bodhisattva not departing from the fundamental, yet manifesting departure from the fundamental in fifteen ways?
What is meant by the bodhisattva attaining nobility, with merit like a treasury in sixteen ways?
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s seventeenth attainment of entry into the Way according to their wish?
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s eighteenth thorough knowledge of all phenomena?
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s nineteenth constant peace and stability in all that they do?
What are the twenty ways in which a bodhisattva acts within the world without attachment?
What is the first way in which a bodhisattva is sovereign in the Dharma and upright, such that none can equal them?
What is meant by the bodhisattva never being separated from the Buddha?
(2) What is meant by the bodhisattva training with settled composure?
(3) What is meant by the bodhisattva’s mind neither grasping nor rejecting any phenomena? (4)
What is meant by the bodhisattva protecting all things (1)?
What is meant by the bodhisattva reaching the turning of the wheel of Dharma (2)?
What is meant by the bodhisattva reaching the stage of *anavaivartika* (irreversibility) up to the rank of *ābhoga* (the ultimate limit) (3–7)?
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Aniruddha!"
The Bodhisattva’s inquiry is indeed such that it enables all beings to find their proper place.
Those present in this assembly, as well as those yet to come, shall all be guided by him; thus this Mahāyāna will endure for a long time.
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall now speak.
Then he said:
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva attains mastery through four matters."
What are the four?
First, his radiance is entirely unimpeded;
second, regarding all precious treasures he possesses, he does not begrudge them to those who seek them.
Third, if one who is learned in the sutras preaches the Dharma without interruption and encourages others at the periphery to do likewise;

fourth, if when requested to preach the Dharma, one does not find it difficult, but rather receives the Tathāgata’s inconceivable inspiration and speaks with joyful exuberance, without harboring any expectations regarding the affairs of bodhisattvas, and bestows the Dharma as a gift.
These are called the four matters.
Furthermore, there are four matters for deeply penetrating all phenomena, such that the activities of one's wisdom are never divorced from merit.
What are these four?
First, one truly understands the twelve links of dependent origination;
second, one cherishes others as one cherishes one's own body, regarding them as no different from oneself;
third, regarding birth and death, one does not think of anything from which they come or to which they go.
All dharmas manifest emptiness through emptiness;
these are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one fully knows the minds of all people and the increase or decrease of their merits.
What are the four matters?
First, entering the Dharma-body without any blemish or defilement;
second, manifesting all the various marks of excellence.
One contemplates the three by means of four matters;
when the mind is without disruption, one attains samādhi.
These are the four matters.
"Furthermore, there are four matters by which one teaches and transforms others in accordance with all their actions.
What are these four?
Their wisdom is equal and uniform;..."
1. To transform all people; 2.
to observe and know all phenomena; 3.
their own minds being already pure and clean, they purify the minds of all people. 4. [This constitutes the fourth.]
These are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one knows the conduct of the transformations performed upon the minds of all people.
What are these four matters?
First, his wisdom penetrates all things without exception;
second, his insight is free from all obstructions;
third, his mind is devoid of duality.
Fourth, having overcome all hindrances during sleep, one no longer clings to them.
These are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which the transgressions and merits one has committed are not forgotten.
What are the four matters?
First, there is nothing whatsoever to be severed;
second, there is also nothing whatsoever to which one may become attached.
Third, knowing causes and conditions, one acts in accordance with what is manifested, upholding the Dharma through the Dharma;
fourth, neither conceiving of a self nor conceiving of a person, one follows these teachings without losing the path of the Dharma.
These are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one adorns oneself through giving.
What are these four?
First, being adorned with the marks;
second, manifesting excellence according to what people delight in;
third, having a most noble and beautiful complexion.
Fourth, that which is performed is inexhaustible.
These are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one uses pure precepts as adornment:
First, he becomes a Cakravartin king without ever forgetting the bodhisattva mind;
second, he becomes Śakra Devānām Indra, adorning himself with the bodhisattva mind;
third, he becomes a Brahmā, his mind adorned by the bodhisattva mind.
Fourth, one leaves all evil realms behind and is born only in the heavens or as a human in the world, adorning oneself with the bodhicitta.
These are the four matters.
"Furthermore, there are four matters that adorn patience.
What are these four?
First, his voice is like that of Brahmā, such that all who hear it each find what they need."
First, his voice is soft and beautiful, like that of the kalaviṅka bird;
second, there is none who does not love and delight in it;
third, he is always firm and steadfast in his meritorious virtues.
These are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one adorns oneself with diligence.
What are these four?
First, his body is like a vajra, such that no malevolent forces can find an opportunity against him;
second, he acts as a benefactor for all beings;
third, he fully accomplishes whatever tasks he undertakes without subsequent regret, and he never tires of study.
There are four things that his mind seeks and fully accomplishes;
these are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which he adorns himself with dhyāna.
What are the four matters?

First, not being obstinate or antagonistic in one's actions; second, not being frivolous or playful; third, not committing wicked or evil deeds; fourth, having self-knowledge and no contrary intentions. These are the four matters.
"Furthermore, there are four matters by which one is adorned with wisdom.
What are these four?
Not conceiving of a self, nor conceiving of a person, nor conceiving of a life-sustaining principle, nor conceiving of a life-force; neither clinging nor severing—these are the first."
Second, that which is performed is most venerable;
third, there is nothing among all existing things that it does not penetrate;
fourth, regarding all dharmas, there is no longer any fear.
These are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one’s wisdom naturally leads to the Brahma Heaven.
What are these four matters?

First, to regard all beings with the compassion of emptiness; second, to teach all people while bestowing upon them pity; third, to encompass all dharmas for the sake of their protection; fourth, to be equal toward all without abandoning the Buddha-nature—these are the four matters.
"Furthermore, there are four matters by which one does not depart from wisdom.
What are these four?
First, dwelling in the four dhyānas without wavering from the state of a bodhisattva."

First, by means of the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the three concentrations (*samādhi*), and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and through the application of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), one is not reborn among the two [higher] formless realms;
second, one possesses mastery over the mind as described, never departing from the Dharma;
third, one reaches everywhere throughout the ten directions, seeing all Buddhas; fourth, [one attains these].
These are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one attains mastery.
What are these four matters?
1. They are extinguished within themselves and likewise extinguished without;
2. They thoroughly understand that all phenomena are like illusions;
3. They take wisdom as their power.
Fourth, attaining liberation without being self-conceited.
These are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are four matters for deeply entering wisdom.
What are the four matters?
First, knowing desire yet not severing desire, and not attaining realization midway;
second, knowing birth and death, yet remaining within it through *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means).
Third, to know all that is seen as being either the way of governance or not the way of governance, yet not abandoning what is seen;
fourth, to know the absence of wisdom and to draw near to the twelve links of dependent origination.
These are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one demonstrates the Dharma to arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and all people, without harboring any expectation therein.

What are the four matters? First, observing all samādhis as being like illusions; second, clearly understanding all dharmas while adorning them; third, delighting oneself with supernormal powers while remaining discerning in one's actions; fourth, knowing within one’s own mind that it is like an illusion. These are the four matters.
“Furthermore, there are four matters by which one neither departs from birth-and-death nor enters parinirvāṇa.

What are these four? First, mindfulness of all Buddhas; second, a mind of universal compassion; third, the employment of *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means); and fourth, not forgetting the original vow made at the time of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment. These are the four matters.”
"Furthermore, there are four matters by which one knows that all people are not separate from the Dharma-body.
What are these four?
To view all people as inherently spontaneous (svabhāva), and to know that the entry of all people into the Dharma-body is likewise spontaneously one; this is the first."
1. To know that all persons are naturally non-dual; 2.
That persons are naturally so and wisdom is naturally so, without doubt; 3.
That persons are naturally so and *nirvāṇa* is naturally so, thereby attaining patience (*kṣānti*).
These are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are another four matters that likewise do not depart from the fundamental, yet perceive within the absence of a fundamental.
What are these four matters?
First, constantly mindful of nirvāṇa and desiring to fulfill the Buddha-dharma, their intention is to possess universal knowledge;
second, manifesting as a Cakravartin, a Brahmā, or a Śakra, they display merits therein to cause those in the assembly to attain this Dharma through these means;
third, manifesting as inferior beings, they cause those who are lowly to be able to perform meritorious deeds.
Fourth, regarding those who have something they seek, one gives them even one's own body, manifesting in a state of supreme nobility and great magnificence to lead and transform them.
These are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one maintains perception while entering the state of non-perception.
What are the four matters?
First, life and death are impermanent, yet his mind remains pure and unified;
second, though suffering has existed from the beginning, he has now attained wisdom.
Third, viewing all dharmas as being without self;
fourth, the tranquility of nirvāṇa.
These are the four matters.
“Furthermore, there are four matters for being free from all views.
What are these four? First, purity;

second, that which the wisdom-eye sees is nothing it does not perceive; third, that the Buddha-eye stands fully before one; fourth, having already crossed over, one is sealed by the *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) stage. These are the four matters.”
“Furthermore, there are four matters through which one gains mastery and resolves all doubts.

What are these four? First, having no obscuration regarding what one desires; second, entering into the wisdom of the truths; third, there being nothing that is not covered [by knowledge]; fourth, never being separated from the various dhāraṇīs. These are the four matters.”
"Furthermore, there are four matters by which one conforms to worldly customs without attachment.
What are these four?
First, to fully understand worldly affairs."
2. One is then able to deliver all people;
3. One has already abandoned both hatred and attachment;
4. By purifying the source, one remains unstained.
These are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one abides in the Dharma.
What are these four matters?
First, mastery over the mind; second, mastery over wisdom; third, mastery over knowledge; fourth, mastery over *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means). These are the four matters.
"Furthermore, there are four matters. What are these four? First, not being separated from the Tathāgata;

second, praising the physical form of the Buddha for the sake of all beings; third, teaching and illuminating others so that they may resolve their minds to become bodhisattvas; fourth, constantly keeping the Buddha in mind. These are the four matters."
"Furthermore, there are four matters through which one knows all phenomena in tranquility.
What are these four?
First, to fully know worldly affairs by means of the Way;..."
First, to clearly comprehend all forms of wisdom;
second, to have no doubt regarding what one has heard and thereby attain the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*);
third, not to dwell on the notions of "existence" or "non-existence," and fourth, not to follow worldly people in their various activities.
These are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one serves as a teacher without being greedy.
What are these four matters?

To act as a cause and condition for all people: first, his mind is simple and sincere, free from flattery; second, he relinquishes his own physical comfort to concern himself with others; third, he does not seek wisdom for his own sake but solely for the sake of all beings—these are the four matters.
“Furthermore, there are four matters that provide protection for all beings.

What are these four? First, sacrificing one’s own body while taking concern for others; second, relinquishing all pleasures to find joy in the Dharma for oneself; third, not forming conceptual attachments to what one hears; and fourth, nourishing and developing oneself through the Dharma. These are the four matters.”
"Furthermore, there are four matters by which one shall attain the turning of the wheel.
What are these four?
First, attaining dharani and attaining the fulfillment of one's own desires."
1) Being without exhaustion or cessation;
2) entering into one's own mind and clearly understanding all phenomena within; 3) fully comprehending others.
4) [The fourth is] fully liberating others.
These are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are four matters that lead even to the stage of *anavaivartika* (non-retrogression).
What are these four matters?
First, they have already crossed over birth and death, yet do not depart from the state of a bodhisattva;
second, because they have attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they undergo birth and death while never departing from the Dharma;
third, they have already obtained the seal of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression).
Having now attained the four seals of the Tathāgata, one has now reached the ten stages of the path; having reached these ten stages of the path, one understands them all in their proper sequence.
These are the four matters.
When the Buddha preached this *Sūtra on the Four Matters of the Bodhisattva*, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and its radiance illuminated everything without exception.
The devas flew above him, providing entertainment and offerings for the Buddha with hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of music, raining down celestial flowers, and all exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
The Buddha has now heard all that he practiced throughout incalculable kalpas.
Those present in this assembly who hear this Dharma have already cultivated merit since the beginning.

Having heard it, they shall recite, chant, and uphold it, and further explain it extensively for all people; their minds shall never forget it. The deeds performed by such bodhisattvas as these shall also be like those of the Buddha.
We have already obtained this benefit.
Why is that? Because we have attained the hearing of this Dharma.

At that time, eighty-four thousand devas and humans all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and twelve thousand bodhisattvas all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The Bodhisattva Aniruddha asked the Buddha:
"After the Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, those who hear this sutra, and who recite it, chant it, praise it, and make offerings to it—how many dharmas of merit shall they obtain?"
The Buddha said:
"One shall obtain eight meritorious qualities:
first, one's faith shall not differ from that of a bodhisattva, and one shall dwell steadfastly in it."
Second, they give their own bodies to others, causing all people to increase in merit without harboring any resentment in their hearts;
third, they abide in infinite great compassion, teaching and illuminating all beings;
fourth, for the sake of the Dharma, they never tire of study and inquiry, just as the ocean is never satiated by the influx of myriad streams.
Fifth, one desires to protect all dharmas;
sixth, by means of the merit of the Dharma, one nurtures oneself so that even though the body dies, it subsequently becomes twice as excellent;
seventh, entering into all meritorious virtues, one fulfills original vows and is protected by all Buddhas.
Eighth, by subduing all Māras, one is freed from fear.
By means of these eight matters, a bodhisattva attains the dharmas of merit after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa.

At that time, the earth of this trichiliocosm shook in six ways and became as level as the palm of a hand. All mountains, hills, oceans, ponds, canals, ditches, and pits appeared as if they were solid ground; even those within the water seemed as they had always been.

Even from the hundred-year-old withered trees, various kinds of leaves sprang forth; those leaves all caused their branches to incline toward the direction where the Buddha was situated, and it was likewise so for all other beautiful trees.
The earth produced lotus flowers as large as chariot wheels, of countless colors, whose radiance completely illuminated and opened up the trichiliocosm.
Looking up from below, one sees nothing at all, yet the sound of music is heard, and its tone is most exquisite.
At that time, the fragrance from the Ice Mountain and the Fragrant Mountain reaches this place, pervading everywhere without exception.
The flowers emerged from this mountain and came down as rain upon the Buddha, covering the ground until they reached the ankles of those standing there.
From the tree under which the Buddha sat, flowers likewise emerged, and the sound of music was heard, just like celestial music.

Above that Buddha’s seat was a precious jeweled canopy thirty thousand *li* in height, covering the throne; between the ribs of the canopy were precious bells surrounding its perimeter, all of which hung with pearls. From the intervals of these hanging pearls, their sounds pervaded the entire trichiliocosm.
Śāriputra came forward, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and asked the Buddha,
"What is the omen of the fundamental cause that has resulted in this manifestation?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

“There is a king named Dundubhisvara, who has come together with incalculable thousands of *dundubhisvaras* from Mount Gandhamādana, with incalculable thousands of *gandharvas*, and with incalculable thousands of devas.”
As these auspicious signs were being described, before the words had even finished, Dṛḍhadhanus was seen approaching together with eighty-four thousand musicians and an incalculable number of people.
The flowers fell from above like rain descending from the heavens.
Together with those who had come with them, they prostrated themselves with their heads to the ground to pay homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and then all stood before him.
King Druma then took up a lute made of lapis lazuli in his hand. Why was this?
Because it was his original vow.
On each side there were forty-two thousand musical instruments, and with Tundila at their center, they all played the lute simultaneously; the sound pervaded the entire trichiliocosm.
Whatever musical instruments the sons of the gods of the desire realm possess, their sounds at that time cannot equal this voice.
Why is this? Because its sound completely overwhelms them, rendering them inferior.
The devas of the desire realm and the devas of the form realm all arrived at the place where the Buddha was.

When this sound was struck, the trees, the famous great mountains, the ice mountains, and King Mahāmeru in this trichiliocosm all quaked and swayed at that moment as if dancing; they all bowed and inclined toward the Buddha, as if a person were performing a prostration.

The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; each of the honored bhikṣus and the bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds; and all the devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits present in the assembly—all leaped from their seats, their bodies bristling with excitement, as if wishing to break into dance.
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra asked:
"Venerable one, you Śrāvakas have already abandoned all desires, have fully attained the eight stages of dhyāna, and have completely perceived the Four Truths.
For what reason do you dance again?"
The venerable śrāvakas replied:
“We have no mastery over ourselves; because of this sound of the lute, we are unable to endure its tone while seated, nor can we restrain our minds to keep them firmly settled.”
The Bodhisattva Aniruddha asked Mahākāśyapa:
"Venerable sir, you are advanced in years and yet you know contentment; you maintain yourself according to the precepts and are revered and loved by both devas and humans."
"Why is it that you cannot control your body's dancing, as if you were a small child?
Mahākāśyapa replied, "It is like when the Sūlana wind arises; all the trees, even those called 'great trees,' cannot control themselves."
Why is this? Their bodies could not endure the sound of King Druma’s lute; it was like the rising of the Sūlana wind. For this reason, we were unable to restrain ourselves.
Now I know that the deeds performed by this Superior One possess merits that cannot be matched.
All that belongs to the śrāvakas is now entirely eclipsed by this sound.
The Bodhisattva Animiṣa again addressed Mahākāśyapa:

"Observe the deeds of those who are *avaivartika*; hearing this sound of the lute, they remain unmoved. How could a person of wisdom, upon hearing this, not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
All the power of the spiritual majesty possessed by the śrāvakas was entirely eclipsed by the sound of the lute; yet this sound could not shake the Mahāyāna.

All the musical instruments and the eighty-four thousand sounds belonging to King Druma were sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, and were also brought about by the merit resulting from Druma’s own original vows.
Of all the sounds of the musical instruments, there was not one whose sound was not heard; they all said:
"All dharmas are equal and entirely liberated; low, middle, and high are all pure and likewise empty, without distinction."
When all people have reckoned that there is no person, it is likewise for the past, the future, and the present; one merely hears its sound, yet realizes that nothing exists at all.
As for that dharma, all human voices are likewise so.
All lands (*kṣetra*) and what is equal to lands are already equalized, yet because there are no lands, they are non-dual.
"That light is non-existent; it is equal to and commensurate with its field, such that there is neither one who is born nor one who grows old.
Therefore, emptiness is without consciousness and is spontaneous (*svabhāva*). All that exists is non-existent; this is the third spontaneity."
“Furthermore, external practice cannot be apprehended, nor can internal practice be apprehended.
That wisdom is fundamentally distinct from dharmas, and even the designation ‘dharma’ is non-existent; its name is likewise so. (4)
5. “One knows that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is non-existent; having practiced without attachment, one attains the peace of the past which is unsurpassed.
6. “Having followed the root of the Dharma as it was heard, one completely destroys all that is non-existent; there is nowhere to go, nor is there anywhere to abide.”
"What they calculate consists only of words; yet, though they fully know the nature of words, they are equal and do not distinguish them as seven.
Because that which the mind sustains is equalized, there is nothing existing; its fundamental transformation does not mutually cognize itself."
That which the mind contemplates is also without arising; one who knows this possesses wisdom and thus enters the eighth dharma.

When the faculties have been equally severed, and the preceding and succeeding dharmas are likewise equal, one whose knowledge is equal across the three periods of time possesses wisdom and thus enters the ninth, which is infinite.
“Ordinary people are bound by the names of forms; this is what ordinary people do—from beginning to beginning, from birth to old age—without end. Once the conditions are known, they no longer cease.”
"To say that there is a self or a person is to contradict the fundamental [teaching]—this is ten.

To abide in equality where there is no abiding, and for all dharmas likewise to have no abiding, such that one knows this abiding in non-abiding—this is the eleventh, rejoicing in hearing and believing."
“Just as when it rains there is lightning, this is the natural state of the higher [reality].
All dharmas are the self; therefore, they are called ‘natural.
Second, the self and persons are naturally empty. One who knows this enters the seal of dhāraṇī and fully understands all gateways of liberation.”
"Because they share the same characteristics, there are three.
As for the 'dharma without characteristics,' it does not exist because it lacks emptiness.
Because it employs characters without expectation, it is distinct from the dharma; thus, there are four [categories]: superior, middling, and inferior."
As for those characters, they are used separately without self-awareness; because they cannot be seen, their minds are already primordial, and that which is primordial continues.
Having known that all dharmas are non-existent, one has already severed the primordial limit (pūrvakoṭi); thus it is fivefold.
"Having severed the fundamental limit (*mūlānta*), one acts for the sake of all beings;
having known that the fundamental limit is equal [to all], this is the sixth aspect of compassion (*karuṇā*).
Having purified compassion, one is then equal toward suffering and pleasure, neither rejoicing nor grieving; such a person is a superior person (*uttamapudgala*)."

Because they have already entered the fundamental nature, those who study the Dharma are tranquil and utterly still; whether they speak or do not speak, there is no increase or decrease in the Dharma. For this reason, they are tranquil and free from longing. (7)
“The voice in the sky cannot be grasped; it can only be heard. There is nothing spoken therein, and both what is spoken and what is heard are not real.
When they heard these words, eight thousand bodhisattvas all attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Bodhisattva Aniruddha asked the Buddha,
"From where does this sound of praise issue forth?
The Buddha replied:
"If you ask King Druma, he will explain it all to you for yourself.
At that moment, having accepted these words, he asked Druma:
"From where does this sound of praise originate?"
He replied: "It issues from the voices of all people.
He asked again:
"From where do all human voices arise?
"They arise from emptiness.
Then the Bodhisattva Vimilaprabha said:
“Dṛḍhadhanu! Do all human voices not arise from the mind?
Dṛḍhadhanu then asked the Bodhisattva Aniruddha:
"Does this sound issue from the body,
or does it issue from the mind? Devadatta replied:
“Nor does it emerge from the body, nor does it emerge from the mind. Why is this?
Because the body is not permanent.”
It is like grass that does not grow constantly, or like a wall that does not remain forever;
there will inevitably be times of its absence. This mind has no form; it cannot be seen, nor can it be perceived, nor can it be heard; it is like an illusion.
Drumakinnara further asked Tiṣya:
"If there is neither body nor mind, from where does this sound emerge?
He then replied:
"All sounds arise spontaneously from thought.
As you have said, sound exists because of thought; yet, the sound of my current praise issues forth from emptiness. Why is this so?"
"Because all sounds are not separate from emptiness.
Then Dṛḍhadhanus said:
"If you, O worthy one, wish to understand sound, know that all sounds exist naturally through emptiness."
One hears the sound but cannot see it, and it immediately ceases.
That which ceases is also empty; therefore, it is called "spontaneous" (*svabhāva*).
The reason all phenomena are equal is that they are equal to space.
That which is spoken and that which is not spoken are also equal. Why is this?
Because emptiness is equal.
All dharmas can only be heard; they cannot be seen.
Regarding the dharmas that are heard, one does not see those dharmas within the hearing.
Just as the sound of the dharma is not seen, this sound likewise does not manifest within the dharma.
All dharmas cannot be awakened to; as for why they can be heard, it is because of *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) that they can be heard, yet there is actually nothing heard.
Through the knowledge of *upāyakauśalya*, one then has no expectations regarding dharmas.
One who has no expectations is firm in essence and firm in power; being no longer weak, they are steadfast and strong, such that nothing can sever them.
That which cannot be severed does not arise;
that which does not arise has no point of attachment.
That which has no attachment is already light;
that which is light is pure;
that which is pure is stainless.
The Dharma has already been attained; it is exceedingly clear and exceedingly luminous.
That which is exceedingly clear is the fundamental nature of the mind; this fundamental nature of the mind is what transcends faults.
Having known the faults once they have occurred, that which has already transcended them is free from conceptualization.
Having transcended all perceptions, that stage is further superior.
This superiority constitutes the patience (*kṣānti*) of a bodhisattva; having attained this patience, there is nothing one does not accept. One accepts emptiness and also accepts persons.
Why is this? Emptiness does not depart from persons.
What, then, is emptiness?
Persons are empty; they endure non-conceptualization and they endure conceptualization.
Why is this so? Because conceptualization is naturally non-conceptualization; likewise, they endure wishlessness and they endure wishing.
Why is this? Because their aspirations are spontaneous and lack any fundamental basis for aspiration.
All dharmas are nirvana, and they likewise exercise patience toward birth and death.
Why is this so? Because birth and death are like a dream.
When a bodhisattva attains patience (*kṣānti*), they do not doubt existence or non-existence; maintaining a single realization, they fully know all people.
By employing patience, one knows that all phenomena neither go anywhere nor come from anywhere, and that all phenomena abide.
Having realized that phenomena abide, one knows that all people likewise abide.
Those who have already entered this Dharma possess the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena; there is only sound.
As for that patient acceptance of the Dharma, it is neither something spoken nor something that can be explained, for its very essence is likewise inexpressible.
“The Buddha is most venerable; it is impossible to preach the Dharma and cause people to attain realization.
The Bodhisattva Aniruddha addressed the Buddha: “How wonderful!

The subtle and wondrous teaching spoken by Dhṛtarāṣṭra is truly marvelous. He has clearly understood and realized the profound Dharma and attained forbearance (*kṣānti*); he is able to enter into the specific forbearances possessed by each of the Honored Ones and inquire of the Buddha about these most profound matters.”
“Since this king has performed such meritorious deeds, how many Buddhas has he served?
His desire for self-indulgence is indeed so great.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Tiyunli:
"One might be able to know the number of sands along the banks of the Ganges, taking each grain of sand to represent a buddha-field, or even the total number of stars filling the heavens;
yet the number of Buddhas served by Tundila is incalculable."
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra asked Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"Since you have served so many Buddhas and accumulated such vast and sublime merit, for what reason do you not quickly attain Buddhahood?"
Then Druma said: "A bodhisattva never tires of ten things. What are these ten? "

1. Serving the Tathāgatas without weariness; 2. The merit one performs without weariness; 3. Studying the Dharma without weariness; 4. Knowledge of the four dhyānas and five abhijñās without weariness; 5. Contemplating all dharmas without weariness; 6. The desire to extensively expound the Dharma without weariness; 7. The desire to instruct all people without weariness; 8. Constantly desiring to protect the Dharma without weariness; 9. Desiring to fulfill all pāramitās without weariness; 10. Desiring to move, transform, guide, and assist others without weariness. These are the ten things in which a bodhisattva never tires.
Ratnottara asked the Buddha:

"I have heard that there is a samādhi of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas called 'Jewel Tathāgata. One who attains this samādhi is fully endowed with all jewels, and whatever Dharma they preach is sovereign."
The Buddha said,
"Listen attentively to what is being taught. Tuṣṭhita said:
"I shall receive your instruction; I only wish to hear it.
The Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva does not exhaust the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha of bhikṣus; by generating the mind of awakening through these three things, there are eighty dharma-treasures."
"What are the eighty?
That his mind does not forget *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is the first treasure;
that his mind does not abandon faith is the second treasure."
That his mind practices all meritorious virtues without indolence is the third treasure;
that his mind is firm and he does not abandon his vows is the fourth treasure;
that whatever he possesses he gives away without any sense of attachment or stinginess, and furthermore increases it, is the fifth treasure.
That his mind acts only with mindfulness of the Bodhisattva is the sixth treasure;
that his mind adorns the body by not transgressing the three matters of the body is the seventh treasure;
and that one whose mind is pure has no evil in speech is the eighth treasure.
His mind is adorned, and his mind does not harbor evil; this is the ninth treasure.
His mind is already restrained by precepts, and adornment is added to his person; he harbors no desire for and does not think of the evil of others; this is the tenth treasure.
His mind is free from all obstructions and treats all people with equality; this is the first treasure.
Their mind is already adorned with patience, enduring all evils; this is the second treasure.
Their mind does not cherish their own body or life for the sake of the bodhisattva path; this is the third treasure.
Their mind is free from hatred or attachment and remains unshakable; this is the fourth treasure.
His mind is firm, diligent, and untiring; this is the fifth treasure.
All that his mind undertakes he desires to accomplish; this is the sixth treasure.
His mental reflections and mental activities are straightforward, and he never forgets what he has done as he seeks to fulfill the bodhisattva’s tasks; this is the seventh treasure.
His mind enters the dhyānas, samādhis, and samāpattis; having brought these forth, his actions become sovereign—this is the eighth treasure.
His mind seeks the Dharma with the desire to harmonize with all forms of wisdom—this is the ninth treasure.
Regarding the Dharma he has heard, he practices its recitation with diligence—this is the twentieth treasure.
That his mind preaches the Dharma without any expectation for gain, because he delivers all who seek it—this is the first treasure;
that his mind is free from artifice regarding the Dharma—this is the second treasure;
that his mind contemplates the right path and acts in accordance with reality—this is the third treasure.
Because his mind hears and acts according to what he has heard with thorough scrutiny, this is the fourth treasure;
because his mind is fully endowed with wisdom and does not follow the teachings of others, this is the fifth treasure;
because his mind possesses boundless compassion and protects itself, this is the sixth treasure.
His mind possesses infinite compassion because it regards all beings with equality; this is the seventh treasure.
His mind possesses infinite protection as he delights in his own Dharma; this is the eighth treasure.
His mind possesses infinite equanimity as it contemplates all phenomena; this is the ninth treasure.
That his mind does not regard birth and death as toil or suffering because he has already entered into merit—this is the thirtieth treasure;
that his mind desires to teach all people, thinking much of others rather than of himself—this is the first treasure;
that his mind never lacks the Dharma and shares it with others, enabling them to obtain and study it—this is the second treasure.
His mind possesses great wisdom such that there is nothing it does not understand; he possesses supernormal powers such that there is nothing they cannot move—this is the third treasure.
His mind draws near to the *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friend) and studies whatever he hears—this is the fourth treasure.
His mind remains far removed from evil teachers and cultivates merit—this is the fifth treasure.
His mind is equal toward all; by practicing this, he has no dualistic mind—this is the sixth treasure.
His mind knows that birth and death are an illness, and thus he enters into the minds of all people—this is the seventh treasure.
His mind acts as medicine for all to cure their various ailments—this is the eighth treasure.
That his mind does not treat those without wisdom with contempt, because he honors the Dharma—this is the ninth treasure;
that his mind is not conceited and endures all things—this is the fortieth treasure;
that his mind is not fawning or deceitful—this is the first treasure.
That his mind does not forget the Dharma he has heard because it abides in the Dharma is the second treasure;
that his mind fully protects all dharmas because he uses mindfulness to repay the kindness of the Buddhas is the third treasure;
and that his mind desires to repay this kindness because it is firm and steadfast is the fourth treasure.
If their mind encounters those who would harm them and yet does not harbor thoughts of retaliation, this is the fifth treasure;
if their mind delights in mountain retreats for the sake of maintaining the purity of the Dharma, this is the sixth treasure;
if their mind constantly desires to leave the household life and become a śramaṇa in order to reach the Right Path, this is the seventh treasure.
When the mind naturally finds fulfillment in the Way, exercising self-restraint and guarding against evil, this is the eighth treasure;
when the mind is content and causes others to each rejoice, this is the ninth treasure;
and when the mind is content with worldly affairs, one does not become weary of the Dharma—this is the fiftieth treasure.
To protect one's own mind and not engage in the clamor of the multitude is the first treasure;
for the mind never to be weary of or satisfied with all merits, employing the primary marks and secondary signs, is the second treasure;
for the mind never to be weary of or satisfied with wisdom, desiring to resolve the doubts of all people, is the third treasure.
Their minds constantly mindfulness of the Buddha; because they do not depart from the Buddha, this is the fourth treasure;
their minds constantly mindfulness of the Dharma; because what they teach does not depart from the Dharma, this is the fifth treasure;
their minds constantly mindfulness of the Saṃgha; because they thereby reach the Saṃgha of the Avaivartika (Non-retrogressive), this is the sixth treasure.
His mind constantly recollects the precepts, remaining unshakable and never departing from the bodhisattva path; this is the seventh treasure.
His mind constantly recollects giving, because he does not crave his own body; this is the eighth treasure.
His mind constantly recollects the heavens, thereby entering the stage of "one birth to full enlightenment"; this is the ninth treasure.
His mind fully knows the origin and thoroughly understands all that exists; this is the sixtieth treasure.
His mind knows the Dharma because it does not destroy the Dharma-body; this is the first treasure.
His mind acts with knowledge according to reality and fully knows everything spoken by all people; this is the second treasure.
His mind knows mastery and satisfies all people; this is the third treasure.
His mind attains *dhāraṇī* and never forgets any Dharma he has heard; this is the fourth treasure.
His mind knows the fundamental Dharma and thoroughly understands all that exists as naturally so; this is the fifth treasure.
His mind guards wisdom and knows that consciousness is like an illusion; this is the sixth treasure.
His mind studies with thorough discernment and attains liberation therefrom without destroying his actions; this is the seventh treasure.
His mind guards the Dharma and desires to know the natural state of persons; this is the eighth treasure.
The mind that knows impermanence and suffering, and is unattached to birth and death within the triple world—this is the ninth treasure;
the mind that views all phenomena as having no self because there is no person—this is the seventieth treasure;
the mind that enters nirvana, which is fundamentally quiescent and further still—this is the first treasure.
Their mind knows emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; having transcended liberation, they are near the gate of *nirvāṇa*—this is the second treasure.
Their mind is without arising; being without arising, it is neither destroyed nor extinguished; those who attain such liberation obtain patience—this is the third treasure.

Their mind knows that things are like illusions, like dreams, like mirages, like echoes in the mountains, and like reflections in water; having realized this, they are firm and free from all expectations—this is the fourth treasure.
When his mind joyfully understands the twelve links of dependent origination and departs from attachment and cessation, this is the fifth treasure;
when his mind perceives all things with complete clarity, yet neither seeks nor falls into duality, this is the sixth treasure;
when his mind does not enter into dualistic matters, but through a single principle fully knows all phenomena, this is the seventh treasure.
That his mind is fully endowed with all practices and does not regress, thereby transcending all forms and names—this is the eighth treasure;
that his mind gradually draws near because he has already perfected the Dharma—this is the ninth treasure;
that his mind unites and gathers the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment to deliver all dharmas—this is the eightieth treasure.
The Buddha said to Druma:
"Once one has practiced these eighty matters and brought them to fulfillment, one attains the Treasure Tathāgata Samādhi.
Having attained this samādhi, one dwells in neither the treasure of the Path nor the treasure of desire."
"What is called the treasure of desire?
What is called the treasure of the Path?
The treasure of desire refers to the various devas and humans—the Honored One among men, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Cakravartins."
If there are venerable lords and princes, each of these noble clansmen has their own preeminence within heaven and on earth; yet once they have attained such status, they do not become arrogant.
To take delight in this and, as a bodhisattva, desire to attain it is called the "desire for jewels.
As for the "jewel of the Way," it is to deliver the mundane through the Dharma.
What dharma is it that delivers worldly beings?
It is the Dharma of the Way. Why is this so?
All that is accomplished through desire is due to wisdom; wisdom is the very image of the Dharma.

It is like how all streams flow back to the great ocean, as Mount Sumeru is the most honored among all mountains, as the moon is the greatest light among the stars, as the sun illuminates all darkness, as the lion is the most fierce among all beasts, as a king is supreme among the masses, as Śakra is the most venerable in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and as Brahmā alone towers above all other Brahmās. Because this wisdom is preeminent among all dharmas, it is called the King of Wisdom.
Therefore, those who wish to cross over attain crossing by means of this, because it is the path of peace and security.
It is like holding up a torch in the darkness to obtain light; its function is exceedingly powerful, subduing all Māras.
He acts as a king of physicians, compounding all medicines;
he acts as a teacher, understanding all matters.
If he holds a bow and a curved horn, where the arrow is aimed, there is nowhere that the arrow does not penetrate.
If a strong man were to take up weapons and strike at something, there would be none who could escape with their life at that moment;
likewise, when one takes up this wisdom to strike against ignorance and delusion, there is nothing that remains unexhausted.
Why is this? Because they have removed defilements.

Their minds are equal and without distinction; they do not contend with others, nor is there anyone who can harm them. They harbor no resentment toward others, for that which they undertake is brought to completion.
Because his wisdom is loyal and substantial, he is able to accomplish deeds of ultimate sincerity; this is the cessation of mental activity.
All things are equal; this is the severing of causes and conditions.
This divine power unites all merits; this is the root.
To act subsequently is power;
to possess wisdom where there was ignorance is awakening;
and to perceive the path of humanity is the Way.

"Being already stilled, one becomes further stilled; being oriented toward contemplation, one contemplates. Within darkness, one acts to create light; when darkness departs, this is precisely what constitutes light.
Because this light is natural, because it is free from defilement, and because it can purify others and liberate them from desire, it is able to release others from their desires."
It is invisible, for having transcended all realms, there are no realms remaining.
Having attained internal stillness, one passes beyond all emptiness by means of entering into emptiness.
Having already abandoned all objects of perception, this is non-conceptualization.
To have nothing sought after in tranquility is the perception of wishlessness.
Having already transcended the three realms, that which is signless is itself the sign, for its sign is equal to emptiness.
Why is this? Because there is no seeking, this constitutes giving;
because one has already transcended "what belongs to me" and "what does not belong to me," being without expectation, this constitutes precept-keeping.
To have no abiding is patience;
to have nothing to grasp and nothing to relinquish is diligence;
to have no increase or decrease is meditative concentration.
That which cannot be known as a location is wisdom.
Everything that is entered is entered by means of wisdom, because it is in accord with *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means).
"It is like a dream; having no self as an adornment, all that is done is merit, and one is already detached and dwells nowhere.
The Buddha said to Dundubhisvara:
"This is the treasure of wisdom. When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with this, they immediately attain the Tathāgata-treasure samādhi."
It is like the great ocean, which receives all streams and treasures; all those named treasures arise from within it.
If a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they likewise receive all people, for the purpose of gathering together all dharmas.
