The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Aniruddha:
“There are thirty-two matters of pure practice through which a bodhisattva fulfills the dānapāramitā.
What are these thirty-two matters?
First, when a bodhisattva practices giving with the desire to seek Buddhahood, the arousal of the resolve (bodhicitta) is the foundation;
second, when a bodhisattva practices giving, they should remain detached from the paths of the arhat and the pratyekabuddha;
third, when a bodhisattva practices giving, they should maintain the thought of wishing to deliver and liberate all people throughout the ten directions.
Fourth, when a bodhisattva gives alms to others, their mind feels no regret;
fifth, when a bodhisattva gives alms to others, they regard them as if they were Buddhas;
sixth, when a bodhisattva gives alms to others, their mind is free from stinginess and greed.
Seventh, when a bodhisattva gives alms to others, his mind is undisturbed and he bestows them with joy;
eighth, when a bodhisattva gives alms to others, he personally measures out the gifts with his own hands;
ninth, when a bodhisattva gives alms to others, his intention is vast and tireless.
Tenth, when a bodhisattva gives alms to others, he does not seek to be reborn anywhere;
eleventh, when a bodhisattva gives alms to others, he harbors no expectations therein;
twelfth, when a bodhisattva gives alms to others, he does not harbor any attachments, following instead the teachings of the Buddha’s sūtras.
Thirteenth, when a bodhisattva gives alms to others, it is because they delight in the Buddha’s sutras;
fourteenth, when a bodhisattva gives alms to others, it is because they desire to seek the path of the Buddha;
fifteenth, when a bodhisattva gives alms to others, they do not become conceited.
Sixteenth, the bodhisattva bestows gifts upon others because he wishes to encourage, exhort, and instruct them;
seventeenth, the bodhisattva bestows gifts upon others because he wishes to deliver and liberate sentient beings;
eighteenth, the bodhisattva bestows gifts upon others because he wishes to uphold the sūtras and the Dharma to teach sentient beings.
Nineteenth, the bodhisattva bestows gifts upon others because he follows the Buddha’s teachings;
twentieth, the bodhisattva bestows gifts upon others because he desires to subdue the retinues of Māra;
twenty-first, the bodhisattva bestows gifts upon others because he desires to seek the accomplishment of attaining Buddhahood.
Twenty-second, the Bodhisattva gives alms to others because he desires to become a heroic and valiant leader among men;
twenty-third, the Bodhisattva gives alms to others because he desires to close off the path of the hungry ghosts;
twenty-fourth, the Bodhisattva gives alms to others because he desires to cause those in future lives to practice giving.
Twenty-fifth, when a bodhisattva gives alms to others, it is because they desire to attain noble status, wealth, and happiness in future lives;
twenty-sixth, when a bodhisattva gives alms to others, it is because they desire to attain the bodhisattva path in every lifetime;
twenty-seventh, when a bodhisattva gives alms to others, it is because they constantly desire to be accompanied by virtuous teachers.
Twenty-eighth, when a bodhisattva gives to others, it is because he desires to maintain a serene countenance toward the people of the ten directions in every lifetime;
twenty-ninth, when a bodhisattva gives to others, it is because he desires to establish the root of the Buddha-way;
thirtieth, when a bodhisattva gives to others, it is because he desires to ultimately achieve the state of a bodhisattva.
Thirty-first, the Bodhisattva gives alms to others because he desires to obtain the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
thirty-second, the Bodhisattva gives alms to others because he desires to achieve the adornment of his sphere and to advance toward the Buddha and enter into all the teachings of the sutras.
These are the thirty-two matters of the bodhisattva’s pure giving; such is the bodhisattva’s practice of the dāna-pāramitā.
There are likewise thirty-two matters of the bodhisattva’s pure practice of the śīla-pāramitā.
What are the thirty-two?
First, the conduct of the Bodhisattva’s body is always pure; this is upholding the precepts.
Second, the Bodhisattva is free from stinginess, greed, anger, and delusion, and the words spoken by his mouth are pure and clean; this is upholding the precepts.
Third, the Bodhisattva’s mind produces clear wisdom and does not deceive the Buddha; this is the upholding of precepts.
Fourth, the Bodhisattva does not follow non-Buddhist paths in the practice of the ten matters; this is the upholding of precepts.
Fifth, the Bodhisattva, whether born in the heavens or the human world, is never separated from the Buddha-way; this is the upholding of precepts.
Sixth, the bodhisattva distances himself from arhats and pratyekabuddhas and removes the mind of frivolity; this is upholding the precepts.
Seventh, the bodhisattva stays far removed from flattery and enters the wisdom of the Buddha; this is upholding the precepts.
Eighth, the bodhisattva studies extensively, making the mind of wisdom supreme; this is upholding the precepts.
Ninth, the bodhisattva directs supreme great compassion toward the ten directions; this is the observance of precepts.
Tenth, the bodhisattva universally protects all people throughout the ten directions so that they are fully endowed [with virtue];
this is the observance of precepts. Eleventh, the bodhisattva never transgresses prohibitions and remains free from shamelessness; this is the observance of precepts.
Twelfth, the bodhisattva is not deficient or impaired; his bodily conduct is always characterized by fear and caution—this is the upholding of precepts.
Thirteenth, the bodhisattva does not commit offenses midway nor transgress his original resolve—this is the upholding of precepts.
Fourteenth, the bodhisattva maintains self-restraint and does not commit various evils—this is the upholding of precepts.
Fifteenth, when a bodhisattva follows the instructions of wise people to deliver others from the evil realms, this is upholding the precepts;
sixteenth, when a bodhisattva maintains the precepts as the foundation for rebirth in the heavens, this is upholding the precepts;
seventeenth, when a bodhisattva desires to fully perfect the wisdom that accords with the Buddha’s wisdom, this is upholding the precepts.
Eighteenth, the Bodhisattva constantly and firmly upholds the precepts and does not transgress the Buddha’s teachings; this is the upholding of morality.

Nineteenth, the Bodhisattva does not harbor self-conceit or treat others with contempt, but constantly restrains himself; this is the upholding of morality. [The nineteenth item is missing from all the various canons.
Twentieth, the Bodhisattva is able to govern his own mind and does not follow after lustful desires; this is the upholding of morality.
Twenty-first: When a bodhisattva maintains the precepts so as not to lose the various sutras of the Buddha, this is called maintaining the precepts;
twenty-second: when a bodhisattva maintains the precepts with faith, encouraging and assisting others in their joy, and without deception, this is called maintaining the precepts;
twenty-third: when a bodhisattva does not commit the transgression of stinginess or greed, this is called maintaining the precepts.
Twenty-fourth, when a bodhisattva maintains the precepts with firm stability and teaches others in accordance with the Dharma, this is the upholding of precepts;
twenty-fifth, when a bodhisattva renounces wealth and property and constantly desires to become a śramaṇa, this is the upholding of precepts;
twenty-sixth, when a bodhisattva delights in dwelling in secluded places and takes joy in the sūtras and the Dharma, this is the upholding of precepts.
Twenty-seventh: The bodhisattva does not crave food, drink, clothing, or bedding because he desires to enter the Way; this is the observance of precepts. Twenty-eighth:
The bodhisattva cuts off all evils and accomplishes all meritorious virtues; this is the observance of precepts. Twenty-ninth:

The bodhisattva remains exposed to the elements with single-minded diligence, distancing himself from his kin and clan, guarding his meritorious conduct and virtues; this is the observance of precepts.
Thirty: When a bodhisattva enters into the practice of profound dharmas without any attachment, this is the upholding of precepts;
thirty-one: when a bodhisattva follows the sequential dharma-practice of the twelve links of dependent origination, this is the upholding of precepts;
thirty-two: when a bodhisattva does not follow any non-Buddhist paths and remains far removed from the four inversions, this is the upholding of precepts.
These are the thirty-two matters of the pure observance of precepts for a bodhisattva; such is the bodhisattva’s practice of the *śīlapāramitā*.
Furthermore, there are generally thirty-two matters of the pure practice of the *kṣāntipāramitā* for a bodhisattva.
What are the thirty-two matters?
First, that a bodhisattva does not crave the body is patience;
second, that a bodhisattva does not begrudge his life is patience.
Third, that a bodhisattva does not harbor thoughts of anger toward others is patience;
fourth, that a bodhisattva accepts all insults and humiliations from others is patience;
fifth, that a bodhisattva feels compassion when seeing those who are exhausted, ill, or weak is patience.
Sixth, that a bodhisattva does not treat those who lack instruction with contempt is patience;
seventh, that a bodhisattva, though naturally noble and honored, is easily moved by others is patience;
eighth, that a bodhisattva, when being robbed or harmed by others, feels neither anger nor resentment is patience.
Ninth, that a bodhisattva harbors no anger or resentment toward others is patience;
tenth, that when a bodhisattva is defeated by others and urged to follow the Lesser Vehicle, their mind does not waver is patience;
eleventh, that a bodhisattva delights in faith in the Buddha-way and their mind remains untiring is patience.
Twelfth, that the bodhisattva’s mind remains unmoved and undisturbed, abiding in purity, is patience;
thirteenth, that the bodhisattva never harbors anger toward others is patience;
fourteenth, that the bodhisattva protects the minds of others so that [anger] does not arise is patience.
Fifteenth, when a bodhisattva always approaches others with a gentle and supple mind, this is patience;
sixteenth, when a bodhisattva always maintains a heart of loving-kindness and compassion toward others, this is patience;
seventeenth, when a bodhisattva does not approach others with a mind of self-conceit or arrogance, this is patience.
Eighteenth, when a bodhisattva humbles himself for the sake of the people of the ten directions, this is patience;
nineteenth, when a bodhisattva does not harbor anger toward others, this is patience;
twentieth, when a bodhisattva maintains self-restraint and commits no transgression, this is patience.
Twenty-first: The bodhisattva constantly restrains his own mind so that no [unwholesome] thoughts arise;
this is patience. Twenty-second: The bodhisattva is able to reproach himself for his own transgressions;
this is patience. Twenty-third: The bodhisattva does not dwell upon the long and short [faults] of others; this is patience.
Twenty-fourth, that a bodhisattva always delights in mindfulness of the Buddha-way is patience;
twenty-fifth, that a bodhisattva always delights in understanding the sūtras and dharmas is patience;
twenty-sixth, that a bodhisattva always loves and delights in the people of the ten directions is patience.
Twenty-seventh, when a bodhisattva constantly desires to bestow gifts upon the people of the ten directions, this is patience;
twenty-eighth, when a bodhisattva constantly maintains a harmonious mind toward others, this is patience;
twenty-ninth, when a bodhisattva always delights in welcoming and assisting others, this is patience.
Thirty: When a bodhisattva constantly follows the sūtras and the Dharma without interruption, this is patience.
Thirty-one: When a bodhisattva hears that there are three types of governance and is neither terrified nor afraid, this is patience.
Thirty-two: When a bodhisattva possesses the wisdom that delights in the joy of non-arising, this is patience.
These are the thirty-two matters of the pure patience of a bodhisattva; such is the bodhisattva’s practice of the *kṣānti-pāramitā*.
There are likewise thirty-two matters for the pure practice of the *vīrya-pāramitā* of a bodhisattva.
What are the thirty-two matters?
First, not severing the Buddha-way is diligence;
second, not severing the sūtras and the Dharma is diligence.
Third, not interrupting the community of bhikṣus is diligence;
fourth, delivering incalculable numbers of people is diligence;
fifth, undergoing incalculable cycles of birth and death without weariness of mind is diligence.
Sixth, one should make offerings to incalculable Buddhas without ever becoming weary; this is diligence.
Seventh, one should perform merits that are beyond calculation; this is diligence.
Eighth, one should study sūtras that are beyond calculation; this is diligence.
Ninth, to teach all people throughout the worlds of the ten directions—this is diligence;
tenth, to bring all people throughout the worlds of the ten directions to fulfillment so that they may all attain the Buddha-way—this is diligence;
eleventh, to provide for all people throughout the worlds of the ten directions whatever they ought to have and to give it all to them accordingly—this is diligence.
Twelfth, to take all that one possesses which is good and give it as a gift to others is diligence;
thirteenth, to fully protect and uphold all the prohibitive precepts is diligence;
fourteenth, to exercise the power of patience with complete gentleness is diligence.
Fifteenth, to fully perfect all dhyānas and samādhis is diligence;
sixteenth, to cause all wisdoms to be fully perfected is diligence;
seventeenth, to adorn oneself with the merits practiced within the spheres of all Buddhas so as to create one’s own sphere at the time of becoming a Buddha is diligence.
Eighteenth, to seek supreme power is diligence;
nineteenth, to completely subdue all Māras and their retinues is diligence;
twentieth, to uphold the Buddha’s sūtras and Dharma and to fully subdue other non-Buddhists is diligence.
Twenty-first: To desire to fully attain the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and all the sūtras and dharmas of the Buddhas—this is diligence.
Twenty-second: To adorn the body, speech, and mind—this is diligence.
Twenty-third: Never to be indolent or weary—this is diligence.
Twenty-fourth: that all undertakings are brought to ultimate completion is diligence;
twenty-fifth: that the mind is always fierce and resolute is diligence;
twenty-sixth: that all cravings and desires are completely cast aside is diligence.

Twenty-seventh: All those who have not yet been delivered shall be delivered; all those who have not yet heard the sutras shall be made to hear them; all those who have not yet attained parinirvāṇa shall be caused to attain parinirvāṇa—this is diligence.
Twenty-eighth: Each and every mark possesses a hundredfold merit and virtue, all of which shall be fully perfected—this is diligence.
Twenty-ninth: All the sūtras and dharmas of the Buddhas shall be protected—this is diligence.
Thirty: to resolve that one shall fully know all the realms of the Buddhas, which are beyond calculation, is diligence;
thirty-one: to always behold immeasurable Buddhas in every lifetime is diligence; thirty-two:

to remain far removed from that which arises from diligence, to be free from body and mind, formless, dwelling nowhere, emerging from nowhere, entering nowhere, and being born nowhere—this is non-arising, and to delight in abiding therein is diligence.
Such is the perfection of vigor in the pure conduct of a bodhisattva.
There are, in total, thirty-two matters regarding the perfection of meditation in the pure conduct of a bodhisattva.
What are the thirty-two matters?
First, that which is contemplated is free from transgression; this is purity.
Second, that which is maintained is without deficiency; this is purity.
Third, not forgetting that which has been discerned is purity;
fourth, departing from frivolous play is purity;
fifth, maintaining self-restraint and contentment is purity.
Sixth, the mind is not distracted by improper thoughts; this is purity.
Seventh, one encourages others to perform meritorious deeds and maintains them with the aim of seeking Buddhahood;
this is purity. Eighth, one does not transgress the six matters; this is purity.
Ninth, being appropriately free from attachment is purity;
tenth, observing both the internal and external is purity;
eleventh, fully possessing the five supernormal powers is purity.
Twelfth, the mind is always supple; this is purity.
Thirteenth, non-attachment to the body; this is purity.
Fourteenth, practicing meditative concentration within; this is purity.
Fifteenth, turning toward entry into the Buddha-way is purity;
sixteenth, distancing oneself from evil people is purity;
seventeenth, that which is entered through the illumination of wisdom is purity.
Eighteenth, to fully enter into the merits that serve as causes is purity;
nineteenth, to cause all sutras and dharmas to be fundamentally joyful is purity;
twentieth, to enter into practice according to the proper sequence is purity.
Twenty-first, the grace of wisdom does not turn back; this is purity.
Twenty-second, being accomplished through *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means); this is purity.
Twenty-third, desiring to fully complete all Buddha-works; this is purity.
Twenty-fourth, to have compassion for all suffering people is purity;
twenty-fifth, not to engage in the affairs of arhats or pratyekabuddhas is purity;
twenty-sixth, to gradually delight in entering and becoming fully endowed with profound wisdom is purity; twenty-seventh, never to grow weary of the meritorious deeds one performs is purity.
Twenty-eighth: that all persons are fundamentally non-existent, and one believes this matter—this is purity;
twenty-ninth: that one fully attains the Buddha-samādhi without distraction—this is purity;
thirtieth: that one enters into the thoughts of all people throughout the ten directions and perceives them all—this is purity.
Thirty-first, to fully know the affairs of gods and humans throughout the ten directions is purity;

thirty-second, just as a king of physicians completely cures the illnesses of people, so too does a bodhisattva who upholds the sūtra-dharma completely cure the birth, death, old age, and sickness of all beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions—this is purity.
The bodhisattva’s practice of the dhyānapāramitā is purified in this way.
There are thirty-two matters regarding the bodhisattva’s practice of the prajñāpāramitā.
What are these thirty-two matters?
First, to desire to attain the various sūtras and dharmas of the Buddha without ever feeling weary is to be lofty and brilliant;
second, to recollect the various sūtras and dharmas in their proper sequence is to be lofty and brilliant;
third, to possess wisdom and discernment is to be lofty and brilliant.
Fourth, the wisdom that does not extinguish the dharmas which serve as causes is called sublime clarity;
fifth, entering into discernment and maintaining the understanding of the five aggregates is called sublime clarity;
sixth, receiving the scriptural teachings through discerning wisdom and understanding their fundamental source is called sublime clarity.
Seventh, skill in the *āyatanas* (bases) and the analytical understanding of wisdom is called sublime;
eighth, skill in the twelve links of dependent origination and the gradual realization of them is called sublime;
ninth, skill in the four noble truths and the thorough knowledge of their cessation is called sublime.
Tenth, to gradually enter the discipline of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñā-upāya-kauśalya*) without following [the path of] *nirvāṇa*—this is called lofty brilliance.
Eleventh, to inwardly contemplate and fully understand all things—this is called lofty brilliance.
Twelfth, to fully understand the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) as it is received through transformation—this is called lofty brilliance.
Thirteenth, to thoroughly understand that all dharmas of the various sūtras are without source of arising is what is called "sublime brilliance.

Fourteenth, the fundamental root of all people is non-existent and their form is inherently pure; to enter into the worldly customs and thereby deliver beings throughout the ten directions is what is called "sublime brilliance.
Fifteenth, all dharmas are but a single dharma, and their fundamental root is nirvāṇa; this is what is called "sublime brilliance."
Sixteenth, all objective realms are but a single objective realm; why is this?
Because they are fundamentally empty from the beginning—this is called "sublime brilliance.
Seventeenth, all Buddhas are but a single Buddha; why is this?
Because the entries into the Dharma-body are incalculable, this is called "high and bright.
Eighteenth: all matters are not fully seen or explained; why is this?
Each has its own name, which skillful means (upāya) should fully know; this is what constitutes high wisdom.
Nineteenth, being unimpeded in protecting wisdom, one is able to answer all those from the countless worlds of the ten directions who come to question; this is what constitutes high wisdom.
Twentieth, having attained all the dharmas of the various sūtras without ever forgetting them, by virtue of having obtained dharanī; this is what constitutes high wisdom.
Twenty-first: To fully awaken to all demonic activities and, upon awakening, immediately distance oneself from them—this is called sublime brilliance.

Twenty-second: All phenomena are like illusions; for example, it is as if a person were temporarily wearing a cage-like body and then sheds it in an instant—all things being devoid of inherent existence are likewise so—this is called sublime brilliance.
Twenty-third: Like what is seen in a dream, like a reflection in water, or like an echo in a deep mountain—all phenomena are exactly like this—this is called sublime brilliance.
Twenty-fourth: All dharmas are empty because they fundamentally have nowhere from which they come; this is called sublime brilliance. Twenty-fifth:
Regarding the thoughts in the minds of people throughout the ten directions and the world, their wisdom reaches them all and they fully know their fundamental nature;

this is called sublime brilliance. Twenty-sixth: By maintaining the power of *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) and spiritual majesty, they enter *nirvāṇa*, yet subsequently reappear within the cycle of birth and death; this is called sublime brilliance.
Twenty-seventh: Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; all phenomena follow these teachings, and one perceives the liberation of them all—this is called "sublime brilliance.
Twenty-eighth: The fundamental source is fixed yet without fixation, and there is nothing to be seen; one fully understands the root of all phenomena. Why is this?
All dharmas are without that which is grasped and without that to which one is attached;

this is called sublime brilliance. Twenty-ninth: attaining complete clarity, being free from the darkness of delusion, and fully obtaining the blazing radiance of wisdom, he preaches the Dharma for the people of the ten directions and delivers them all;

this is called sublime brilliance. Thirtieth: knowing thoroughly that all birth and death fundamentally come from nowhere and go nowhere, he follows worldly customs to enter among them and preach the Dharma for the people of the ten directions, manifesting such things as being born again and dying again; this is called sublime brilliance.
Thirty-first, regarding the four things that need no protection: their wisdom reaches its full extent and they know all things universally; this is called being lofty and brilliant.

Thirty-second, when preaching the Dharma to people of the ten directions, they teach according to the sequence and in accordance with what each person delights in; they should restrain their own minds and protect their own wisdom, fully accomplishing and perfecting them all. All Buddhas behold these men of high talent from afar and, for the sake of the Bodhisattvas, maintain the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power to provide complete protection.
This perfection of wisdom is thus pure through thirty-two matters.
There are thirty-two matters regarding the conduct of a bodhisattva’s skillful means (upāyakauśalya).
What are the thirty-two matters?
First, teaching the people of the world in the ten directions to protect their own bodies;
second, those with much merit do not abide therein, nor do those with little merit abide therein.

Third, one should teach the people of the world throughout the ten directions who seek the bodhisattva path, while not teaching those who do not seek it; yet one regards them all as no different from one's own teacher.
Fourth, one constantly desires to bestow many rare treasures and wealth upon the multitude.
Fifth, one always delights in seeking out and imparting extensive teachings to others.
Sixth, manifesting as a woman’s body to teach many women;
seventh, manifesting as a youth to transform children;
eighth, manifesting in various forms of persons out of compassion for the people of the world.
Ninth, when there are those in the world who are deranged, he also manifests a deranged body to deliver them in peace and security;
tenth, if there are those with distracted minds and mental agitation, he preaches the Way of the Sūtras to them according to their agitation;
eleventh, he follows the preferences of people throughout the ten directions to deliver them by means of upholding the Dharma.

Twelfth, even if one has maintained the prohibitive precepts for a hundred or a thousand years, if there is someone who desires to joyfully relinquish the precepts, one goes to teach and deliver them;

thirteenth, according to what people prefer—whether it be clothing, various sounds, music, or entertainments—one provides these as gifts so that they may obtain them, ensuring they are without fail joyful, and then proceeds to teach them by means of the sutras and the Dharma;
fourteenth, as the dhūta practitioners and śramaṇas each have different aims and conducts, one goes to teach them in accordance with their respective practices of the Dharma.
Fifteenth, he enters among the Nirgranthas, Pāśupatas, and other non-Buddhists according to their respective types to instruct them, leading them into the Buddha-way.

Sixteenth, among courtesans he manifests as one of exquisite beauty to become the most distinguished among them; he teaches all these women to abstain from lust, and further transforms himself into men to gradually lead them into the Buddha-way.

Seventeenth, when great assemblies perform various musical performances and there are spectators who listen to the sounds of the music with universal joy, he uses the sounds of that music to preach the Dharma; none of those who hear it fail to attain deliverance.
Eighteenth, he manifests as artisans and performers of the world, entering among them all to teach and transform them so that they may follow the path of Buddhahood;

nineteenth, he manifests as a *pañcavārṣika* festival, and when there are those in the world who are impoverished, weak, and inferior, he points out hidden treasures buried in the earth and bestows them upon the poor, finally preaching the Dharma to them all so that they may resolve their minds [upon enlightenment];

twentieth, when there are those in the world mourning the dead with wailing and grief-stricken by suffering, he likewise manifests through his majestic spiritual power and also manifests grief-stricken himself, teaching and transforming those grieving people so that they may enter the Way of the Sūtras.
Twenty-first: When people in the world have lost their wealth and goods, the Bodhisattva manifests and reveals hidden treasures, teaching them to apply themselves to the Way.

Twenty-second: If there are kings, ministers, or *gṛhapatis* who, being childless, are afflicted by grief and distress, he then manifests entry into their wombs as a son; for each such parent and family, he preaches the sutras so that they may attain liberation. Twenty-third: Among merchants, he is the most noble;

when their provisions are exhausted midway, he manifests his majestic spiritual power to provide his companions with water and food until they are full, and for their sake, he preaches the Way of the sutras.

Twenty-fourth: If there are people born blind upon entering this world—whether a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand—they likewise manifest through their majestic spiritual power so that all these blind people may see. They provide them with clothing, bedding, food, and drink as they require, causing all the blind to regain their sight; none fail to rejoice. Thus, he gradually preaches the Dharma for them, causing them all to resolve to seek the Buddha-way. Twenty-fifth:

In a great city, if there are prisoners bound and confined in a jail, he likewise manifests himself as a prisoner. Within each of those prisons, he employs his majestic spiritual power to cause all those who are imprisoned to receive bathing, clothing, bedding, food, and drink. He preaches the sutras for them all, causing them to resolve to seek the Buddha.

Twenty-sixth: If there are those facing the death penalty who are being led outside the city, the Bodhisattva, by means of his majestic spiritual power (*ṛddhibala*), transforms people in number equal to theirs to take their places. He leads the condemned away, and they are thus released. Greatly rejoicing and filled with joy, he provides them with food and drink until they are full and gives them clothing. He then preaches the Way of the Sūtras to them; having been liberated and experiencing joy, they all resolve to seek the Buddha-way. Twenty-seventh:

If there are disputes, quarrels, or lawsuits—whether over money and wealth or over fields and houses—the Bodhisattva mediates between the two parties from the center. If one side is lacking, he uses his own wealth to effect a reconciliation, providing what is needed to restore balance. Afterwards, he preaches the Way of the Sūtras to them, causing them to resolve to seek the Buddha-way.
Twenty-eighth: Through *upāyakauśalya*, the bodhisattva constantly manifests an upright appearance to people while acting out ugliness. Twenty-ninth:
He manifests as a pitiable śramaṇa to teach people, and further manifests as a layperson (*avadātavasana*) to teach them.

Thirtieth: Practicing *upāyakauśalya*, the bodhisattva remains far removed from those of other paths; he adopts their dress and speech and, within their assemblies, slanders the Buddha, slanders the Dharma, and slanders the Saṅgha of bhikṣus, gradually taking up the sutras and the Dharma to instruct and lead them into the path of the Buddha.
Thirty-first, he gradually teaches others to enter parinirvāṇa and likewise follows them into parinirvāṇa; having entered parinirvāṇa, he immediately manifests again, appearing in other regions.

Thirty-second, practicing *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), the Bodhisattva manifests transformations according to what is pleasing to those he seeks to convert: he may manifest as an arhat, or manifest as a pratyekabuddha, or appear as a bodhisattva, or manifest as a Buddha.
"This is the purity of the thirty-two matters of *upāyakauśalya*.

When the Buddha spoke this *prajñāpāramitā*, the Cūḍapanthaka and his retinue, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas—ninety-three thousand people in all—vowed to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, the eight thousand bodhisattvas who had come with the Buddha all attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*.

King Druma, having attained the Samādhi of Luminous Wisdom, was filled with joy and exultation upon hearing what the Buddha had spoken; he then offered celestial silks to the Buddha, the value of which could not be measured in this world.

At that time, eight thousand people from the palace of the Tuṣita-deva king offered thousand-petaled flower canopies to the Buddha. By means of his majestic spiritual power, the Buddha caused all these flower canopies to appear in the void above the Buddha’s head, merging into a single canopy four thousand li in length and breadth.
When the son of Druma and all the ladies-in-waiting beheld this majestic spiritual transformation, they all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and addressed the Buddha:
"May the Tathāgata instruct and illuminate us, so that we may attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
When he had spoken these words, the Buddha rose forty cubits above the ground and sat in mid-air, emitting from his body a radiance that illuminated the trichiliocosm.

The drums and musical instruments of all the Cūḍāmaṇi and Mahārājika deities, along with their retinues, as well as those of the gods of the desire realm and the gods of the form realm, resounded spontaneously without being struck; on the mountains of fragrant flowers, all the flowering and fruiting trees produced the sound of lutes, their tones being most exquisite.

The Buddha raised the hairs of his body; from each hair there issued forth light containing lotus flowers, and upon each lotus flower sat a bodhisattva, all of whom possessed the thirty-two marks of a great man.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, the sounds of all the musical instruments were heard only as the preaching of the sutra, and they all produced melodies that addressed difficult passages of the sutra—just as people might have doubts. Upon each lotus flower sat a bodhisattva who posed questions on these difficult passages of the sutra, resolving all their uncertainties.
Various sounds issued forth, saying:
"How does one give rise to the practice of the bodhicitta so as not to forget it, and thereby personally attain the seat beneath the Bodhi tree?
The bodhisattva replied:
"When his mind is joyful, he then possesses infinite great compassion toward all; for this reason, he does not forget the two.
His voice then asked again:
"What is the meaning of this?"
"What is the cause?
How is it that, having already attained supreme great compassion, one gives rise to the three?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"His intention is without flattery; that which he relies upon is in accordance with wisdom; and through supreme great compassion, he attains Nirvana.
His voice asked again:
"Regarding what is given in charity, how is it considered truly given?"
How does one act without regret?
How does one not seek that which arises?
What are the five aspirations of a bodhisattva?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"I do not cherish any possessions; once I have given them away, I have no sense of regret.
Because I constantly keep the path of the Bodhisattva in mind, I do not seek to be reborn in any place—this is the sixth [perfection]."
That voice asked again:
"Regarding the pure precepts one has cultivated, how does one avoid being conceited about those precepts?
How does one instruct those who have lost their precepts?"
"How does one personally attain the Mahāyāna?
The bodhisattva replied:
"Wherever there is a virtuous mind, there is pure precept."
"Because one knows that all phenomena are empty, one does not become arrogant.
Because one practices immeasurable great compassion, one is able to instruct those who have lost their precepts.
His voice asked again:
"If there are those who revile, beat, or seek to kill one, how can there be patience?
What state of mind is it that does not arise [in response] and yet finds joy? (9)
The Bodhisattva replied:
"One should think:
'When I become a Buddha, I shall act as a King of Physicians for all people; I shall heal whoever is ill.'"
"For this reason, one is able to practice patience.
Even when there is verbal abuse, beating, or an attempt to kill, no resentment arises in the mind, and instead there is joy.
His voice asked again:
“How can diligence reach its ultimate?
How does one achieve the bodhisattva practice without indolence?
The Bodhisattva replied:

"Regarding diligence: because it employs the Dharma and desires to protect all beings, it reaches its consummation; because it thoroughly understands the reality of emptiness, it is without weariness.
The various voices asked again:
"How should one intend it so that the mind may be fully prepared and enter deeply?"
"What is meant by 'knowing for oneself that there is nothing to be hoped for regarding dhyāna'?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Because the mind is not deluded, one is able to be fully endowed [with all qualities]."
Because his mind is without flattery, he enters deeply;
because he employs *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), he is able to practice dhyāna.
For these reasons, he has no expectations whatsoever—this is the fourteenth.
The various sounds asked again:
"How does one attain the direct course of what is seen through wisdom?
How does one fulfill the karmic activity of the wisdom of the Dharma?"
"How should one resolve these fifteen doubts?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"One who delights in study increases their wisdom; by understanding the twelve links of dependent origination, one is able to practice with directness."
"Because he delights in giving the Dharma as a gift, he resolves all doubts and clearly understands their root—this is the sixteenth.
The various voices asked again:
"How does one possess great wisdom and enable oneself to attain this through hearing?"
"How does one teach others and thereby personally attain the state of the Honored One?
The Bodhisattva replied:

"By constantly practicing humility and self-effacement, one gains great wisdom; by acting upon what one has heard, one can achieve this state; and by giving the Dharma without expectation of reward, one can reach the state of the Honored One. (18)
The various voices asked again:
"Regarding that which is called 'loving-kindness' (maitrī), how does it extend even to the ultimate great compassion (mahākaruṇā)?
How is the possession of the [four] protections (rakṣā) achieved?"
"How does one attain the Brahma-heaven?
(19) The Bodhisattva replied:

"That which is an impartial mind is loving-kindness (*maitrī*); that which is free from weariness is protection (*karuṇā*). Because this mind is thereby joyful and glad, one is able to reach the Brahma-heaven" (20).
The various sounds asked again:
"How can a bodhisattva see the Buddha?
Having seen him, how does one rejoice?"
"What is it that allows one to hear the Dharma without doubt? Twenty-one.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Because his mind constantly recollects the Buddha, he is able to attain the sight and hearing of the Dharma."
"Because his mind is pure and clean, he is able to be free from doubt—this is the twenty-second.
The various voices asked again:
"How can merit be accumulated?"
How is this wisdom to be unified?
How is it known through directed contemplation?
How are these twenty-three matters to be sought?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"One never tires of merit; therefore, one gathers learning without weariness, and thus is able to bring forth wisdom.
When the mind is undisturbed and free from discursive thought, this constitutes the twenty-fourth stage of progress toward contemplation."
The various voices asked again:
"As for 'concealment,' where does it reside?
What is its practice?"
"What are the twenty-five objects of focus?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"That which is 'empty' (zang) is devoid of anything existent."
As for that state, the perfections and the four dhyānas are its practice; its object of focus is to transcend all twenty-six [categories].
Again, the various voices asked:
"What is called the work of Māra?"
"What is meant by 'Buddha-work'?
How does one proceed until the twenty-seventh stage of a bodhisattva?
The bodhisattva replied:
"To lack courage and be timid is, therefore, the work of Māra.
To follow the mind of the Mahāyāna is, therefore, the work of the Buddha.
By completely abandoning all evils, one attains the twenty-eighth stage of a Bodhisattva."
The various voices asked again:
"How should one draw near to a *kalyāṇamitra*— translated in Chinese as 'good friend'—
and how should one distance oneself from an evil teacher?"
"How does one dwell in equanimity?
How does one relinquish twenty-nine?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"To instruct one in the bodhisattva path is to be a kalyāṇamitra;
to cause one to abandon the bodhicitta is to be an evil teacher.
To know for oneself what has been done is therefore to abide in equanimity."
"To abandon the various heterodox views of external paths—this is the thirtieth principle of governance.
The various voices asked again:
"How may all dharmas be protected?"
"How can all people be taught?
How does one employ *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) to bring them to fulfillment in the path of a bodhisattva? The Bodhisattva replied: [31] "... (The thirty-first item.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Because of diligence, one is able to protect the Dharma;
because of *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), one is able to instruct others.
By providing guidance according to whether people are monastics or laypeople, one accomplishes the thirty-two marks of a supreme Bodhisattva."
The various voices asked again:
"In what way does one employ wisdom through one's actions?
What constitutes the work of Māra?"
"How does one exercise vigilance so as not to lose the proper timing?
(33) The Bodhisattva replied:
"One acts so that there is no fault; therefore, whatever is done with wisdom is not unrighteous, whereas what is contrary to the Dharma is the work of Māra."
"Constantly following their teachings is what constitutes being diligent and cautious; always possessing humility and self-effacement, one is respected by others—this is thirty-four.
The various voices asked again:
"What is that Way like?"

"What is that which is not the Way? How does one create a person and cause them to enter the Way? The Bodhisattva replied: "There are thirty-five [factors]. He continued: "What are they? The Bodhisattva reported, saying: [He listed them. "These are called the thirty-five factors for creating a person and causing them to enter the Way. The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent! You have well explained these thirty-five factors for creating a person and causing them to enter the Way. The Buddha then spoke a verse: "The thirty-five factors for creating a person and causing them to enter the Way Are what the Buddhas of the three times all practice. If one practices them with diligence and without negligence, One will surely attain the path of the Buddha. The Buddha then addressed the assembly: "This is called the Dharma-gate of the thirty-five factors for creating a person and causing them to enter the Way. If there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma-gate and, having heard it, believe and accept it, they shall never again fall into the three evil realms. If there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma-gate and, having heard it, cultivate it according to the teaching, they shall surely attain the stage of non-retrogression. If there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma-gate and, having heard it, teach it extensively to others, they shall surely attain the stage of the irreversible wheel-turning king. The Buddha then spoke a verse: "If one hears this Dharma-gate of the thirty-five factors And believes and accepts it with a single mind, They shall never again fall into the three evil realms; This is the supreme teaching of the Buddhas. When the sons of the King of Tuṣita heard this Dharma, they attained the joy of faith and patience (*śraddhā-kṣānti*). Each of them took the precious jewels from their own bodies as an offering to the Buddha, and each spoke these words:

Each addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How truly marvelous!

These sounds of music have posed such questions, and all the manifested bodhisattvas seated here have resolved their difficulties; those present in this assembly are now free from doubt. For our sake, you have opened up countless darknesses and caused us to attain clarity."

The Buddha said:
"All this is brought about by the Tathāgata.
If I wished to cause empty space to produce sounds, it could always be accomplished; how much more so, then, musical instruments and the various trees?"
"For this reason, the deeds performed by the Tathāgata are incalculable.
The sons of the Tuṣita devas all said,
"May all people become just like the Tathāgata."

The Buddha said:

What is this one practice?"
To give rise to the aspiration for *sarvajña* (omniscience) and, having performed immeasurable meritorious deeds, not forget them—this is the first matter.
Furthermore, there are two matters by which a woman may quickly attain manhood and personally realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
What are these two matters?
Acting as one speaks and not serving other deities but taking refuge only in the Buddha;
acting in accordance with what is correct and not believing in what is false—these are the two matters.
“Furthermore, there are three things by which a woman may quickly attain manhood and personally realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What are these three things? They are:
purifying the three ways of guarding the body, the four ways of guarding speech, and the three ways of guarding the mind. These are the three things.”
“Furthermore, there are four things by which a woman may quickly attain manhood and personally realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

What are these four? To practice giving without flattery; to observe the precepts without flattery; to constantly guard oneself without flattery; and to listen to the Dharma without flattery. These are the four things.”
"Furthermore, there are five things by which a woman may quickly attain manhood and personally realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

What are these five? They are: practicing according to the Dharma; acting in accordance with the Dharma; hearing the Dharma and abiding uprightly in it; having no delight in being a woman; and constantly mindful of becoming a man. These are the five things."
“Furthermore, there are six things by which a woman may quickly attain manhood and personally realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

What are these six? They are: being free from indolence; not forgetting what one has undertaken to do; having a supple mind; being simple and honest without flattery or deceit; being devoid of affectation; and being sincere in all that one does. These are the six things.”

“Furthermore, there are seven matters by which a woman may quickly attain manhood and personally realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. What are these seven? Constantly recollecting the Buddha so as to attain the Dharma-body;

constantly recollecting the Dharma so as to attain the Buddha’s wisdom; constantly recollecting the Saṅgha with the desire that they come to belong to one; constantly recollecting the precepts with the desire to purify what is sought; constantly recollecting giving so as to remove all defilements; constantly recollecting the heavens with the desire to make them like the mind of a Bodhisattva; and constantly recollecting humanity for the purpose of crossing over birth and death. These are the seven matters.”
"Furthermore, there are eight matters by which a woman may quickly attain manhood and personally achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

What are these eight? She does not take pleasure in food and drink; nor in flowers; nor in incense; nor in various beautiful and variegated colors; nor does she go to places of amusement and spectacle; nor does she seek pleasure through performers and musicians; nor does she sing or dance. These are the eight matters."
"Furthermore, there are nine matters by which a woman may quickly attain manhood and personally realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
What are these nine? They are:

neither severing anything, nor clinging to anything; not conceiving of a self, nor conceiving of a person, nor conceiving of a life-span, nor conceiving of a soul; not conceiving of that which is born, nor conceiving of that which is unborn; and believing in causes and conditions. These are the nine matters."
“Furthermore, there are ten things by which a woman may quickly attain manhood and personally realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

What are these ten? They are: practicing universal loving-kindness; not being greedy for profit; not coveting other things; never deceiving others even at the cost of one’s own life as a man; refraining from double-tongued speech and delighting in verbal abuse; not speaking falsely; finding no pleasure in performing music or entertainment, nor giving rise to such thoughts; remaining upright without harboring resentment; and not seeking to know matters of perverse sin or merit through worldly means. These are the ten things by which a woman may become a man and quickly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
“Mother, if one possesses a mind of generosity and a mind of Dharma, one regards all forms as clusters of foam upon water and does not become conceited regarding form.

Consciousness is like an illusion; regarding the mind and its intentions, they are seen as no different from an illusion.
One has no attachment to any phenomena, yet through the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—one knows all things.
Just as a house is established by three factors—having grass, having earth, and having wood.
