He heard that among the devas and humans there was no difference, for there were only names.
"The lifespan of that Buddha shall be ten small kalpas, and he shall take an immeasurable multitude of bodhisattvas as his saṃgha; all of them shall attain inconceivable and sublime attainments."
When this Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa, he shall first bestow the prediction of enlightenment upon a bodhisattva.

That bodhisattva is named Udāyin; he shall later become a Buddha, titled Mahodāyin (which in the Han language means "Great Adornment"). This eon is called Rādhāsapti—because there is no end to his devotion toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, it is therefore named Rādhāsapti.

When Druma received this prediction of his future enlightenment before the Buddha, he immediately leaped for joy and flew up into the air to a height of one hundred and forty *zhang*, remaining there so as to bring delight to all those present in the assembly.
Relying on his own merit and through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, he spoke this praise:
"All dharmas are fundamentally pure like space; they are naturally non-existent, and because they are natural, they are without defilement."
One who knows this is the supreme son of the Buddha. First:
"That which is seen in a dream cannot be obtained; therefore, it cannot be grasped, being like empty space."
Knowing that all phenomena are like dreams, one does not regard birth and death as the duality of toil and suffering.
It is like a magician who manifests something; therein, nothing can be apprehended.
Regarding those five aggregates, they are like an illusion in three ways.
That which is form is fundamentally like foam upon water;
that which is sensation is like bubbles upon water.
Furthermore, that which is naturally conceptualized is like a mirage or a plantain tree; nothing is to be found therein.
Within birth and death, nothing is to be found—this is the fourth [point].
That which is known by the mind and intellect consists merely of words.
The Buddha said:

"If one regards them as like an illusion, one knows that the five aggregates are fundamentally empty. One treats birth and death as equal to that which has already ceased; one treats the four great elements as equal to a scale; and because one treats what has already ceased as equal to poison, there are five."
"The six decays are like a desolate wilderness;
having already maintained the Buddha’s majestic power according to the Dharma, one who has subdued themselves bestows [giving]. To act thus is to attain peace;
that which is already pure is itself precept."
When perceptions have ceased, there is patience;
being able to self-restrain and remain tranquil constitutes the seventh [perfection], diligence.
To act without differentiation is what is called dhyāna.
Because there is no obstruction regarding the object of perception, it is wisdom (*prajñā*);
upholding these trainings constitutes the eight *pāramitās*.

Absence of self and absence of person is excellent compassion (*maitrī*); that which is pure is pity (*karuṇā*); its tranquility is like protection (*rakṣā*); practicing with equanimity is the ninth [stage], the supreme Brahma-heaven.
One bestows various gifts through four matters and receives from the Buddha;
through patience one does not become angry, and once greed has ceased, all ten transgressions are eliminated.
It is likewise with the absence of self and life-span; the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are empty and entirely quiescent.
Those who know this are the eleventh type of bodhisattva.

A bodhisattva does not harbor expectations; they do not conceive of there being people or no people, nor do they conceive of there being a self or no self. Because their mind is non-dual, they are without attachment—this is the twelfth.
“The Dharma is non-existent and has no basis; it departs without going anywhere and comes from nowhere. It abides in the Dharmakāya without obstruction.
A Tathāgata is equal to a Buddha in thirteen respects.”
It is neither existent nor non-existent; it exists only due to causes and conditions.
Like lightning that appears and then vanishes, so too is the mind—this is the fourteenth [verse].
Within birth and death there is activity, yet that mind cannot be seen.
The mind is like the wind, having no attachments.
That mind is fundamentally pure; knowing that the mind is fundamentally pure, it remains unstained by birth and death. 15.
"If a fence, wall, or rampart is constructed from earth, grass, and wood, its body is devoid of cognition.
It is like the purity of a stone; the body has no aspirations. (16)
"If the wind cannot be apprehended, its sound is likewise so.

If there is the sound of music and entertainment within a mountain, the knowledge of that sound is also pure; herein, one does not give rise to desire regarding the resonance—this is the seventeenth."
"If one is like space and does not fall, having no abode and no location;
and if one fully knows that all phenomena are like space, having no abode and no place of rest—one who knows thus has already attained the eighteenth equal dwelling."
"Just as a great conflagration cannot burn or scorch empty space,
so too one who knows that all phenomena are pure like space will not be harmed by a great fire even if they travel to other distant lands and realms."
Having realized this Dharma, one no longer regards Mount Sumeru or Mount Cakravāḍa as obstacles;
one who knows this is able to traverse all buddha-fields.
The four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—are entirely equal, for they are empty in nature.
19. Those who know this can reach billions upon billions of lands. 20.
Within the three realms there are sounds—superior, middling, and inferior—and though these sounds have existed for ten billion eons, they have no end, for they are fundamentally natural.
“The Buddha’s form, mind, and so forth are as subtle as a scale, because they are pure through their application.
The equality of all Buddhas is like a scale—this is twenty-one.
When Bodhisattvas have practiced, they assemble immeasurable merits.”
"Having already known that all phenomena of the wholesome mind are entirely equal, one is subsequently able to receive the prediction [of enlightenment]. Twenty-second:
'The Bodhisattva’s own realm is utterly pure within the Dharmakāya.'"
Those who understand this shall subsequently receive their prediction [of enlightenment], number twenty-three.

"One does not conceptualize form, nor does one conceptualize perception; one does not conceptualize feeling, volition, mental formations, or consciousness. It is by virtue of the Dharma that one receives the prediction."

One who receives the prediction of enlightenment does so not because of the five aggregates or the four great elements; emptiness is as perfectly level as a scale. Knowing this is that which arises from nowhere, one subsequently receives the twenty-fourth prediction.
"Those who have reached exhaustion cannot know it themselves;
those who have not yet reached exhaustion cannot know exhaustion;
as for those already tending toward exhaustion, they receive their prediction [of enlightenment] only after the stage of dharmakṣānti."
Those without conceptualization follow the direct path;
those with conceptualization enter the path of error.
To be unattached to all phenomena and to have transcended the three periods of time—those who know this attain the twenty-fifth resolution.
"Knowing that the self is *svabhāva* (natural), one knows that all phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely *svabhāva*;
that there is no self and it is *svabhāva*, being *svabhāva* because of emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
and that what is empty is *svabhāva* and non-existent. One who knows that the three hindrances are equal and empty—therefore, it is called *svabhāva*."
Regarding those who know they have received the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa), one should not understand it in that way, for it would involve the presence of expectation.
To know that there is neither mind nor thought in receiving the prediction—this is the twenty-sixth [aspect] of receiving the prediction.
Rddhimitrā said to those in the assembly:

"While you all remain upon the ground and I am in the void, those who understand that the mind is equally poised upon the ground and in the void—remaining impartial throughout the three periods of time without attachment—are [the ones who truly dwell]. (27)
The Druma-kinnara-rajā, having praised these words, descended from the void and approached the Buddha, saying:
"It is for my sake that the Buddha now exists in this world; the Buddha has explained everything for me."
"My vow has already been fulfilled; having practiced the bodhisattva path for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have not forgotten my merits, and now I have heard them all.
At that time, the various bodhisattvas in the assembly each had this thought:
"From which past Buddha did Tun-jhen-t'o-lo (Dundubhisvara) originally resolve his mind [on enlightenment]?"
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts of the bodhisattvas and wishing to resolve their doubts, called out to the bodhisattva Aniruddha and said:

"In the past, incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Ratanaketu—which in the language of Han means 'Jewel-Flower. His buddha-field was named Śūka; śūka, in the language of Han, means 'pure appearance. That kalpa was named Pāralina; pāralina means 'pure aspect.'"
At that time, the Tathāgata had twelve billion bodhisattvas, all of whom were diligent, had attained forbearance, and were all *avaivartika*.
The lifespan of that Buddha was sixty billion years.
The adornments of that buddha-field are such that nothing is left unaccomplished.
Its ground is entirely made of lapis lazuli, and no grains are sown there.
Should anyone experience hunger or thirst, exquisite food and drink appear before them in their entirety.
In that land there were no other paths; all followed the Mahāyāna.
At that time, there was a Cakravartin king named Nimi-dhara, who ruled over the four quarters.
This Cakravartin King made offerings to the Buddha and sixty billion bodhisattvas for a period of one trillion years; the merit he thereby produced was immeasurable.

Together with his eighty-four thousand wives, his thousand sons, and his eighty-four thousand officials and attendants, he all simultaneously resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Having thus resolved their minds, they continued to serve and honor the Buddha for another hundred million years.
Afterwards, he installed his son—named Huatopolin—as the regent and established him as king; he then renounced the kingdom and went forth to become a śramaṇa.

That prince who was established as king likewise made offerings to the Buddha for the same number of years as before, and having again installed his own son as king, he too renounced the kingdom and went forth to become a śramaṇa.
In this manner, they shall transmit it to one another in succession according to the aforementioned method, until the end of the Buddha’s lifespan.
After that Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa,
the final and last king shall uphold and maintain the Dharma.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Tiwuli:
"Do you know King Nimi of the Cakravartins?
The one currently manifest as Duntendhalo is he."
Then Aniruddha said: "Excellent, excellent!
The Buddha’s wisdom is such that he knows and explains all things throughout the immeasurable and incalculable long eons."
The Buddha said:
"This wisdom is not worth mentioning. Why is that?"

He is able to know the mental activities of all persons—past, future, and present—including those with causes and those without causes, and those with merit and those without merit; therefore, the wisdom of the Tathāgata is unimpeded.
When the Buddha spoke these words on being without hindrance, eighty-four thousand people all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
After the Cūḍāmaṇi-dhara (Tunzhentuo) and his palace retinue had made offerings to the Buddha for seven days, they took their entire kingdom and presented it to the Buddha, saying:
"All of this belongs to the Tathāgata."
"From time to time, may the World-Honored One come to this place out of compassion for all beings.
Then the Crown Prince Indradatta—whose name was Vimukta—offered a canopy of interlaced maṇi jewels to the Buddha and said:
"Now I, Indradatta, have great desire for music and dance; I only pray that the Buddha will illuminate us with the teaching of the Dharma, so that we may become free from desire for music and dance."
The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I shall provide protection for your mind. Whenever there is the sound of music and performance, I will cause you to hear the sounds of the sixty-four dharmas according to where you are directed."
What are the sixty-four dharmas? They are:

merely hearing the sound of impermanence, the sound of suffering, the sound of emptiness, the sound of non-self, the sound of tranquility, the sound of purity, the sound of the absence of birth-and-death, the sound of primordial purity, and the sound of that which is unarisen from any source. As it is...
The sound of the fundamental nature, the sound of the ultimate limit, the sound of original non-existence, the sound of the Dharma-body, the sound of the Tathāgata,
the sound of no person, the sound of no life-span, the sound of no vital principle, the sound of no coming,
the sound of no future, the sound of no past, the sound of no present, the sound of no location, and the sound of non-attainment.
The sound of voice, the unsurpassed sound, the sound of generosity, the sound of pure precepts,

the sound of patience, the sound of diligence, the sound of single-mindedness, the sound of wisdom, the sound of loving-kindness, the sound of compassion, the sound of protection, the sound of equanimity, the sound of the Buddha,
the sound of the Dharma, the sound of the Saṅgha, the sound of the non-forgetfulness of bodhisattvas, and the foundations of mindfulness.
The sound of voice; the sound of the severance of mental activity; the sound of the bases of psychic power; the sound of the faculties; the sound of the powers;

the sound of the factors of enlightenment; the sound of entering the path; the sound of resonance; the sound of contemplation; the sound of *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means); the sound of the fourfold mixed giving;
the sound of teaching all beings; the sound of protecting the Dharma; the sound of subduing Māra; and the sound of illusion.
The sound of dreams, the sound of what is seen in dreams, the sound of sunlight, the sound of echoes, the sound of reflections in water,
the sound of the indestructible Dharma-body, the sound of the ten powers, the sound of the four fearlessnesses,
the sound of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the sound of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and the sound of non-retrogression.
The sound of reaching [the goal], and the sound of adorning the buddha-fields—these constitute the sixty-four matters.

Through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, all musical instruments produce only the sound of the Dharma; those who enter into this immediately attain the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
At that time, everyone in the assembly was filled with joy; they all prostrated themselves, touching their heads to the ground, and each said:
"The Bodhisattva is most venerable; those who abide in the Dharma are all protected by the Buddha."
The Buddha said:
"O assembly! It is as you have said."
"Those bodhisattvas who abide in the Dharma are all protected by the Buddha. Why is this?
Because to protect a bodhisattva is to protect all people.

Why is this so? Because the Bodhisattva’s aspiration is for the sake of all beings; therefore, it is called *saṃnāha* (the great armor). He protects those who are ignorant and deluded, liberating them from birth and death, so that they all reach *nirvāṇa*.
The Buddha said:
"One who knows how to protect a bodhisattva has already protected all people.
If one gives to a bodhisattva whatever they require—whether it be possessions, alms bowls, or robes and garments—it is as if one has given to all."
Why is this so? Because it is through the exhalation and inhalation of breath that a bodhisattva maintains life.
It is just as when a person has exhalation and inhalation, by means of which they are able to remain alive; [the bodhisattva does this] because he desires to benefit all beings.

The entire assembly—the devas of the desire realm, the devas of the form realm, the Śuddhāvāsa devas, the Cāṇdālas, the Gandharvas, and the Mahoragas—all praised and supported the words spoken by the Buddha, and each took various flowers and scattered them over the Buddha.
Drumakinnara thought to himself, "The bhikṣus, bodhisattvas, and even the Buddha shall all return.

Wishing to cause them to return by means of his own supernormal power, he immediately manifested a jeweled lattice chariot three hundred li in length and breadth, entirely composed of various jewels, with countless precious gems forming its trees.

For the Tathāgata, he prepared a lion throne four zhang and nine chi high, adorned with celestial silks of countless colors and spread with fine carpets upon all the seats, and caused the bhikṣus and bodhisattvas to each take their respective places.
For the sake of Śakra and the four Brahmā kings, he prepared seats like those of the devas; having thus completed them, he addressed the Buddha:
"I have prepared these with great compassion; please accept them."

The Buddha, together with the community of bhikṣus and all the bodhisattvas, boarded the chariot of the *Cūḍāmaṇi* (Tunzhentuo). At that moment, by means of the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the *Cūḍāmaṇi*, they rose one hundred and forty *zhang* above the ground; the chariot traveled through the void, followed by eight thousand devaputras, as well as all the *Cūḍāmaṇis* and *Gandharvas*.
Druma-kiṃnara, together with his retinue, pulled the jeweled lattice chariot with golden cords as it proceeded directly toward the road.
The Buddha emitted a radiance that illuminated the entire trichiliocosm.

When King Ajātaśatru, along with his ministers, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, saw the radiance and knew that the Buddha was about to arrive, they all took silken banners, parasols, streamers, flowers, and incense and went out from the city of Rājagṛha, all emerging together to go forth and welcome him.

Eighty-four thousand musical instruments of the Druma-kinnara played in concert; as they moved along, the sound of lutes and harps was heard first. Then Druma, together with his sons and retinue, pulled the chariot to escort the Buddha.
Upon arriving at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the Buddha descended from his carriage and took his seat; the bhikṣus and bodhisattvas all stood before him.

King Ajātaśatru, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, each of the venerable ones, and those among the scattered vassal kings who were subjects of Ajātaśatru, all holding silk canopies, flowers, and incense, made offerings to the Buddha and paid him homage; each of them addressed the Tathāgata, saying:
The Bodhisattva Animiṣa asked the Buddha:
"What merit shall Ṛddhimantatāla and his retinue obtain for having escorted the Buddha here by means of their chariot?"
The Buddha said:

"As for those among the Druma-kinnara-rāja and his retinue who have resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, by virtue of this merit they shall all attain the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā), and shall not forget them until they attain Buddhahood."
From one land to another, they shall make offerings to all Buddhas and likewise listen to their teachings.

They shall perceive that all members of the bhikṣu-saṃgha possess knowledge of past lives and shall all achieve supreme great compassion; they shall always protect the Dharma and always teach and transform all people.
King Ajātaśatru said to Druma:
“Excellent, O benevolent one!
You are praised by the Buddha.”
King Ajātaśatru replied again to Druma:
"I pray that you share with me a small portion of the merit you have cultivated, so that I may obtain its benefits."
Rddhimitrā then replied:
"If it pleases you, I shall take these merits and bestow them upon you and all people. Why is this? Because..."
All the merits performed by a bodhisattva are for the sake of all beings; he harbors no attachment toward them.
Regarding the merits he performs, he does not think, "This was done by me alone," but allows it to be shared by all people.
Whatever the bodhisattva does, he acts so that all may receive its blessings and protection.
"Why is this? Because a bodhisattva is the causal condition for all beings; by gradually training himself, he is able to benefit others.
Thus, Tuṣṭimdhara said to Ajātaśatru:
“Excellent, O virtuous one!
You have obtained two kalyāṇamitras:
the first is the Buddha, and the second is Mañjuśrī.”
"By receiving this grace, all my doubts regarding the unrighteous acts I have committed shall be completely dispelled.
King Ajātaśatru said, "The deeds of the Bodhisattva are most excellent;
he has already become a vessel for the Dharma by nature, such that his mind harbors no doubt toward whatever Dharma he hears, nor does he conceptualize it, nor does he forget it."
The Bodhisattva Devadatta asked the Buddha,
“What is meant by a bodhisattva being able to serve as a vessel for the Dharma?
The Buddha said:
"One becomes a vessel for the Dharma by means of thirty-two matters.
What are these thirty-two matters?
That a Bodhisattva dwells firmly and is protected by the Buddhas is the first matter of being a vessel for the Dharma."
Their intention is not deceitful and their speech is consistent; they have faith in merit—this is the second quality of a vessel for the Dharma.
They practice the deeds of a bodhisattva—this is the third quality of a vessel for the Dharma.
They apply their minds to what they have heard—this is the fourth quality of a vessel for the Dharma.
Having entered the mind, one gradually approaches the Way; this is the fifth vessel of the Dharma.
Entering the knowledge of all fundamental origins is the sixth vessel of the Dharma.
Attaining honor through giving is the seventh vessel of the Dharma.
Being fully endowed with pure precepts and fulfilling one's vows is the eighth vessel of the Dharma;
the patient person attaining the thirty-two marks is the ninth vessel of the Dharma;
and the diligent person [attaining] all the qualities of the Buddhas is the tenth vessel of the Dharma.
One who possesses single-mindedness cures their illness; this is the eleventh vessel of the Dharma.
One who possesses wisdom is free from all obstructions; this is the twelfth vessel of the Dharma.
One who possesses loving-kindness treats all people with equality; this is the thirteenth vessel of the Dharma.
That which is compassionate protects all who are impoverished; this is the fourteenth vessel of the Dharma.
That which is protective feels compassion for all people; this is the fifteenth vessel of the Dharma.
That which possesses an impartial mind treats all beings with no difference in its heart; this is the sixteenth vessel of the Dharma.
To act as a kalyāṇamitra for others is the seventeenth vessel for all dharmas of merit;
to never tire of what one hears is the eighteenth vessel for the prajñāpāramitā;
to become a śramaṇa and, though separated from parents and kin, not cease to apply oneself with diligent effort in the mind is the nineteenth vessel for the Dharma.
To delight in mountain retreats and dwell alone with a concentrated mind—this is the twenty-second vessel of the Dharma;
to be able to endure solitude and thereby attain the stages of dhyāna—this is the twenty-first vessel of the Dharma;
to give away one's own possessions to those who have nothing and thereby instruct others—this is the twenty-second vessel of the Dharma.
To protect all dharmas and cause those who are blind and in darkness to obtain clarity—this is the twenty-third vessel of the Dharma;
to know the *dhāraṇīs* and, understanding their matters, being able to guide others—this is the twenty-fourth vessel of the Dharma;
to resolve the doubts of all people according to what they desire—this is the twenty-fifth vessel of the Dharma.
Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha will swiftly attain a vision of the Buddha; this is the twenty-sixth vessel of the Dharma.
The twenty-seventh and twenty-eighth dharmas are missing from all extant editions;
those who are free from anger and whose minds harbor no resentment possess merit that can never be exhausted—this is the vessel of the Dharma.
Having realized the nature of emptiness and having no longing for anything that exists, this is the thirty-first vessel of the Dharma;
understanding thoroughly the faults and attachments of the twelve links of dependent origination and departing by severing them, this is the thirty-second vessel of the Dharma;
having attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), this is the thirty-third vessel of the Dharma.
That they will receive the prediction of enlightenment before long is the thirty-first vessel of the Dharma;
that they remain unshakable and immovable through the power of their progress toward *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) is the thirty-second vessel of the Dharma.
"These are the thirty-two matters that constitute a Bodhisattva’s vessel for the Dharma.
When this was said, ten thousand people all resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and they all raised their voices, saying:
"May all beings without exception obtain such a vessel for the Dharma, and may we ourselves attain the vessel for the Dharma as taught by the Buddha."
The Buddha said to Dundubhisvara, "You may return to your abode; do not cause people to toil.
Dundubhisvara replied:
"One whose mind dwells on weariness is not a bodhisattva;
one who does not dwell on weariness is a bodhisattva.
Then, Druma again asked the Buddha:
“What is it that causes a bodhisattva to conceive weariness?
What is it that prevents a bodhisattva from conceiving weariness?
The Buddha said:
"A Bodhisattva can be known to have exertion through four matters.
What are the four matters by which exertion is known?
Hearing of countless people, their hearts become terrified; this is the first exertion."
To hear that one cannot cross over birth and death and for the mind to be terrified by it is the second weariness;
to hear that the wisdom of all Buddhas is immeasurable and for the mind to be terrified by it is the third weariness;
to hear that innumerable merits constitute a single mark and for the mind to be terrified by it is the fourth matter of knowing and yet having weariness.
"A Bodhisattva knows through four matters yet does not become weary.
What are these four?
To desire to deliver all people and cause them all to reach Nirvāṇa—this is the first matter, and one does not consider it wearisome;..."
To wish to protect oneself from the immeasurable coverings of birth and death, and to wish to cultivate merit with a mind free from fear—this is not weariness.
To hear of the immeasurable wisdom of the Buddhas and wish to fully possess it all with a mind free from fear—this is not difficulty.

To hear that immeasurable merits are perfected as a single mark and have a mind free from fear, continuing to cultivate merit without regarding it as difficult—these are the four matters by which one knows a bodhisattva does not undergo toil.
"Furthermore, there are four matters by which one knows and reckons their diligent toil. What are these four?
From time to time, they take pleasure in the affairs of the śrāvakas and go to attend upon them."
In the interim, they take pleasure in the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas and draw near to them;
when the various dharmas are about to perish, they pay no heed and offer no protection;
nor do they instruct others to resolve upon the mind of a Bodhisattva.
These are the four matters by which one knows that a bodhisattva considers their efforts to be laborious.
Furthermore, there are four matters for which one cannot consider there to be labor. What are these four?
They do not take pleasure in the dharmas of Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas;
they listen to the Dharma even at the cost of their own lives, never departing from it;
and if they hear of a good person who can be inspired to the Bodhisattva mind, they go to teach them, regardless of how great the distance.
These are the four matters by which one knows that a bodhisattva does not become weary.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one may know that there is weariness.
What are these four?
If there are śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or impoverished beggars who come with some request, he immediately turns toward them in anger;
he is concerned only with obtaining food, drink, and restful sleep, and pays no heed to others;
he pays no heed to study or learning.
"I shall be one of great knowledge," yet whenever he hears wisdom at various times, he departs in haste and does not wish to teach it to others.
These are the four matters by which one knows a bodhisattva who reckons his efforts as laborious.
"Furthermore, there are four matters by which one knows [the practice] yet does not calculate it as toil. What are these four?

When a beggar comes with a request, one bestows a gift upon them, regarding them as if they were a *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend); one's mind is supple, and one maintains a pleasant countenance toward all."
Not thinking of one's own bodily ease, but desiring only to bring peace to others;
never becoming weary or satisfied in one's training;
teaching all people according to what one has heard, without any expectation of reward.
These are the four matters by which one knows that a bodhisattva does not reckon their labors as wearisome.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which a bodhisattva reckons their labors as wearisome. What are these four?
They do not seek the path of the *pāramitās*;
they do not practice giving by means of the four bases of sympathy;
and they desire to instruct all people in the way to proceed, even though those people lack diligence.
"Having already heard and reflected upon what is to be heard, one considers it sufficient and does not contemplate the Bodhisattva path.
These are the four matters by which one knows that [the Bodhisattva] calculates there is weariness.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one may know that the Bodhisattva does not calculate there is weariness."
What are the four matters?
If one’s body is set ablaze with fire, one does not consider it a grievance; likewise, in seeking the various *pāramitās*, one does not succumb to indolence.
One bestows the four kinds of gifts and always remains fully prepared, never turning away those who come to seek them.
To desire to bring joy to others through diligence;
to desire to be endowed with all merits, knowing them yet never becoming weary—
these are the four matters by which a bodhisattva knows how not to calculate their own toil.
The Buddha said to Ajātaśatru:
"Having heard of the Bodhisattva, do you not consider it a labor?
He then replied:
“I have heard it.
The Buddha said,
“As for those who have heard it, from this day forward, those who practice as bodhisattvas must not grow weary of what they do, nor calculate their toil to the extreme.”
King Ajātaśatru asked the Buddha,
"What is meant by the practice of a bodhisattva? Thereupon,
the Buddha spoke among the assemblies of the Cūḍapanthaka, Gandharvas, and others:
"Each has attained their respective place.

When Ajātaśatru heard the Buddha’s teaching on the bodhisattva practice, he acted according to what he had heard of the Dharma; thus, he practiced the bodhisattva path without calculating its hardships."
He practices with an equanimous mind toward all, with firm conduct, and with truthful conduct; his mental actions are pure, and he acts without guile regarding the Dharma of the bodhisattvas.
The practice of giving, the practice of generosity, and the practice of being without attachment to anything whatsoever.
Performing the conduct of a bodhisattva, they do not perform the practice of pure precepts based on any objective support.
They practice tranquility and the purity of body, speech, and mind; having already brought this to mind, they constantly practice patience and act by relinquishing all resentment.
One who practices the conduct of a bodhisattva does not give rise to thoughts regarding the practice of vigor.
Whatever actions they undertake, they do not proceed with weariness or hardship toward saṃsāra; in performing the conduct of a bodhisattva, their mind is neither timid nor weak.
One practices through meditation, one practices through knowledge, and one acts with a settled body and mind; thus, in performing the bodhisattva practice, the mind remains undisturbed.
A bodhisattva should act with wisdom according to the Dharma, and in practicing as a bodhisattva, they do not calculate that there is anything to be attained.

The practice of loving-kindness, the practice of a gentle mind, the constant practice of compassion, and the practice of what a bodhisattva performs—namely, the practice free from anger; the practice of emptiness, the practice with intention, and the practice of pure non-conceptuality; the bodhisattva’s practice is one of wishlessness. This is the practice that a bodhisattva should perform: the practice of fulfilling the wisdom of the mind.
“The conduct of a bodhisattva consists of unimpeded conduct of faith, conduct of diligence, and conduct of the samādhi of settled mental application.
That conduct of a bodhisattva consists of uninterrupted conduct of the bases of spiritual power, conduct dedicated solely to purposeful effort, and conduct by means of the five supernormal powers.”
The deeds performed by a bodhisattva are not unwholesome deeds; they are deeds of impartial practice, deeds of the vehicle of the Dharma, and deeds performed with the desire to instruct all beings.
Such are the deeds performed by a bodhisattva: they are deeds that do not rely on causal conditions, deeds performed according to reality, and deeds that sever all darkness.
Regarding the deeds of a bodhisattva, they practice without error, pure conduct, and conduct that liberates from all defilements; such are the deeds a bodhisattva performs.
They practice with freedom from regret and tranquility, and protect all beings so that they have no fear; such are the deeds a bodhisattva performs, thereby fully accomplishing all that is desired.
Walking like the sun, walking like the moon, and walking like a lotus flower unstained—when a bodhisattva practices in this way, they are revered by all the devas.
When a bodhisattva practices such conduct as the conduct of Śakra, the conduct of Brahmā, and the conduct of the complete path, all Māras are struck with fear.
When a bodhisattva practices such conduct as the conduct of upholding, the conduct of honoring, and the conduct that exhausts lust, anger, and delusion, incalculable devas all praise them.
“Practicing what is practiced, practicing for a long duration, and practicing with the eye of wisdom purified—when a bodhisattva practices in this way, there is no expectation.
Practicing tranquility, practicing with solemnity, and practicing without attachment to name-and-form—when a bodhisattva practices in this way, there is no fault.”
When a bodhisattva performs such practices, they are praised by all the devas.
"Speaking with gentle words, acting with equanimity, and abandoning false paths—these are the practices of a bodhisattva."

Taking wisdom as the fundamental practice, the courageous practice, the practice of shaking all Māras, and the practice of never deviating from sitting beneath the Bodhi tree; the practitioner who attains *dhāraṇī* performs whatever actions a bodhisattva undertakes without weariness.
“Practicing in mountain retreats, practicing with endurance, and always delighting in the desire to perform the conduct of a śramaṇa—this is the conduct of a bodhisattva.

Practicing with a mind that acts according to the causes for liberation, practicing with reverence toward all things, practicing with unimpaired eloquence regarding the objects of a bodhisattva’s focus, practicing with *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), practicing without expectation regarding the dhyānas and *kṣāntis*, performing the bodhisattva’s practice of non-dharmas, practicing among the mundane, practicing beyond the mundane, and practicing within the realms of desire, form, and formlessness—a bodhisattva who performs such practices is fearless; there is nothing they do not practice, and they fully know the conduct of all people.”
“32. The conduct of a bodhisattva is like that of heaven, for there is nothing it does not cover.
When the Buddha spoke these words on the conduct of bodhisattvas, five hundred bodhisattvas all attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Within that assembly, eight thousand people all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and they all spoke to the Buddha, saying:
"We shall all practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, exactly as it should be practiced."
The Buddha manifested a miraculous response, wishing to cause Druma to return to his own abode.

At that time, Druma, together with his palace and retinue, circumambulated the Buddha three times; they knelt before him in prostration to take their leave, emitting bodily radiance and performing various musical performances, playing lutes and harps. The earth shook in six ways as celestial flowers rained down, and they then returned to their place, entering their palace.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now that Druma has made offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṃgha of bhikṣus, and the bodhisattvas, his merit already surpasses my own."
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
“It is not only that he surpasses you; his merit already exceeds that of all the Śakras, Brahmās, and Cāturmahārājikas throughout the trichiliocosm, as well as all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”

Why is it so? Because as soon as a bodhisattva has once resolved their mind, they surpass all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all ordinary people; for they shall attain liberation by means of that Dharma.
“The Bodhisattva excels all; there is none who can surpass the Buddha, and thus we know that there is no one who can surpass the Bodhisattva. Why is this so?
“The Buddha attained his realization because of the Bodhisattva mind; all Śrāvakas attain their realization because of the Buddha-dharma.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, Śakra-devānām-indra shed tears and said to the Buddha:
“I have now suffered a loss, for I originally did not resolve to develop the Bodhisattva mind.”
At that time, there was a son of heaven in the assembly named Bhayadarśin, who said to Śakra Devānām-indra:
"In the Buddha-dharma, there is no one throughout the heavens who does not resolve to attain the mind of a bodhisattva."
Now that you have this regret, what further benefit would it bring?
Why is this so? Because you have scorched the seeds of the bodhisattvas, you are no longer a vessel for the Dharma of a bodhisattva.
When Kūṭadanta spoke these words, five hundred devaputras of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Kūṭadanta-devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I have seen that when the Buddha was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, he received a prediction from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*. Now, Tathāgata, you likewise possess such joy in the dharma and patience; I pray that you will explain it, so that we may now hear it from the Buddha.”
The Buddha said:
“A bodhisattva who lacks merit cannot hear the patience regarding the joy in the dharma of non-arising.
The Buddha spoke to Kātyāyanīputra:
“A bodhisattva attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena through four matters. What are these four?

First, knowing that all Buddhas—whether of the past, future, or present—are not one; second, knowing that all phenomena are without distinction; third, equalizing all buddha-fields; and fourth, equalizing all people. These are the four matters.”
“Furthermore, there are four matters. What are these four?

First, delighting in emptiness while knowing the four dhyānas; second, delighting in the three realms of existence through boundless compassion; third, delighting in the six pāramitās through upāyakauśalya; fourth, delighting in the five supernatural powers through wisdom. These are the four matters.”
“Furthermore, there are four matters.
What are these four?
To seek the bodhisattva path within the five aggregates, while the bodhisattva knows that the five aggregates are naturally one;”
First, seeking the Bodhisattva within the four great elements while realizing their natural spontaneity;
second, believing in the four great elements and seeking the Bodhisattva within the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍāyatana*), viewing the six sense-fields as naturally spontaneous;

third, seeking the Bodhisattva within all phenomena (*dharmas*) and realizing that all phenomena are naturally spontaneous; fourth, regarding all phenomena as naturally spontaneous and remaining free from doubt.
These are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are another four matters.
What are these four?
By abiding in the ultimate limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), one knows that all phenomena are one;
having already abided in the Tathāgata, there is no phenomenon into which one does not enter, and one views the three periods of time as equal;
entering into the Dharma-body, one fully knows that the characteristics of all phenomena are like emptiness and indestructible.
To view all phenomena as entirely equal and without distinction— this is the fourth.
These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva attains the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

When this was said, five hundred bodhisattvas all attained the joy of the dharma of non-arising, and the Tathāgata-jñāna-darśana-avatāraṇa-devaputra attained the patience with dharmas (kṣānti) without doubt.
When this discourse on desire had concluded, the Buddha called Ānanda:
"Have you fully grasped what the Dhṛtarāṣṭra asked?"
Ānanda replied, “I have fully attained it; how excellent!
This Dharma is truly peerless and joyous; it is profoundly deep and subtle, just as was originally taught.”
"By this one knows the source and thoroughly understands all phenomena.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
"As for the Dharma as it was originally heard, now that I hear this, I am able to understand it all completely."

Now, if my śrāvakas, upon hearing this, all fully comprehend this Dharma, how much more so the bodhisattvas, whose wisdom is boundless, whose minds are like the ocean, receiving nothing they do not take in;
whose wisdom is exceedingly vast, encompassing everything it does not exclude.

There is nothing among all phenomena that they do not encompass; they serve as a great vessel for all treasures; and for all who have no patron, they act as patrons. If one regards them with such profound wisdom, it is unfathomable.
Ānanda asked the Buddha again:
“Will those who hear this hereafter attain the illumination of the Dharma?
The Buddha said:

"Now, the light from a single hair-pore of the Tathāgata completely eclipses the brilliance of the sun and moon throughout the trichiliocosm; yet even the light from all the hair-pores of the Tathāgata’s body does not equal the attainment of this illumination of the Dharma, for there is nothing this certainty cannot penetrate."
Why is this so? All who possess illumination attain it through wisdom.
One who possesses the illumination of the Dharma knows all people; therefore, he is honored as the one without obstruction.

Thereafter, all who hear this shall attain wisdom and clarity; they shall then uphold, recite, chant, read, and teach it to others. Because they do not depart from the Bodhisattva through their knowledge of the Dharma for the sake of all beings, they take up the great armor (*mahā-saṃnāha-saṃnaddha*) out of infinite compassion, and don the armor of loving-kindness to subdue the various Māras, gradually drawing near to the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now, having received the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, I shall uphold this Dharma; what would be the merit of one who recites, chants, reads, and extensively explains it for all people?"
The Buddha said:

"Suppose there were someone who filled the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system with the seven treasures and gave them as a gift to srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and up to the Buddhas, and continued this meritorious deed for a thousand years."
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"Are its merits not very great?
Ānanda replied:
“Very much, very much,
O God among Gods!
the Buddha said.
"It is not as good as for a man or a woman to practice the bodhisattva deeds and recite, chant, and read them three times each day and night.
If one explains the matters within these teachings to others, their merit exceeds that [of the former], let alone one who speaks such a Dharma as this."

Why is this? Because a bodhisattva explains the meaning within the sūtras for others by means of the four matters found therein; therefore, this constitutes the gift of Dharma—the most honored among all gifts—and is thus the supreme benefit. The gift of Dharma is the supreme protection.
Why is this? Because through the gift of Dharma, when one hears and listens, the defilements of the mind are removed and one attains liberation.
Giving away material possessions merely nourishes the cycle of birth and death; those who wish to transcend birth and death should give the gift of Dharma.
This is what it means to practice the gift of Dharma in accordance with the Buddha’s teachings; all people derive merit from this.
When a Bodhisattva practices the gift of Dharma, they attain thirty-two matters.
What are the thirty-two matters?
First, being settled in one's mental application;
second, being settled in one's actions.
There are three [types] regarding conduct;
four are few regarding sensual desire;
five are rare regarding anger.
Delusion is likewise sixfold;
being liberated oneself and further liberating others from birth and death is sevenfold;
and being beloved by others is eightfold.
Ninth, they are praised by the devas;
tenth, they are protected by nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas;
eleventh, they transcend [the world] through their actions.
Twelfth, they shall obtain robes, alms bowls, bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
thirteenth, their fame shall spread far and near such that there are none who do not hear it, and they shall ultimately never fall under the sway of evil;
fourteenth, they shall be praised by all Buddhas and shall be able to practice the protection of the Dharma.
15. By means of this, one attains the Dharma-body and does not fear the evil realms;
16. One does not regard gods or humans as difficult obstacles;
17. In whatever place one is born, one is never separated from the Buddhas and their teachings.
Eighteenth, upon being born, one immediately knows one's past lives;
nineteenth, one is beloved wherever one is born;
twentieth, one’s body is never deficient or impaired.
21. He immediately attains the thirty-two marks;
22. he attains the *dhāraṇīs* that destroy desire;
23. he understands all causes and conditions and nourishes himself through dhyāna.
Twenty-fourth, one rectifies the path with great wisdom;
twenty-fifth, one brings clarity to those who are in darkness and afflicted by disease;
twenty-sixth, one’s mind is free from deviant thoughts.
27. Being superior to worldly gifts and bestowals; 28.

Being inexhaustible regarding the treasury of the Dharma (dharmagañja); 29. [Being] according to one's desires; 30–32. The four dharmas—these four items are missing from all extant manuscripts—and these constitute the thirty-two.
Śakra Devānām-indra addressed the Buddha:
"I shall receive and uphold this Dharma.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, should there be anyone who is a fit vessel for the Dharma, I shall protect them and cause them to hear this teaching."
"Why is this? It is because one rejoices in the merits described in such a sūtra.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, Śakra Devānām Indra!
Before me, you are as courageous as a lion; you have declared that you shall protect this Dharma in the future.”
By virtue of these merits, even if an asura should come with an army, he would not dare to confront him.
Why is this? Because this essential dharma cannot be attained by anyone.
"And if one wishes to protect it, it is because that which has fear sees nothing erroneously.
One has no expectations regarding the Dharma; therefore, this constitutes protection.
Brahmā addressed the Buddha:
"In whatever commanderies, kingdoms, districts, towns, or villages this Dharma is preached, we ourselves shall abandon our respective abodes and go there to provide protection."
"And why is this? It is because Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śakras, and Brahmās attain their own self-perfection by means of this Dharma.
The Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha:
"We are the disciples of the Buddha; we shall all practice this Dharma and protect it so that it may endure for a long time.

As for those who are our lords and do not believe in the Buddha-Dharma—whether they be nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, or mahoragas—if there are any among them who lack faith, I shall cause them to believe."
They all said: "In accordance with their local customs, we shall recite this mantra:

'Tobhi om bhi a-rye bhi ba-śa-rye bhi hū-yan-ma-hū-yan i-yan kien-yan a-ho-ti wei-yue-ti pa-li-mien-to-na-ni muen-mien pa-kia-san-na yi-ho yi-ho wei-li-ai-mien ta-mien ta-ma-lo-i-to. We shall cause everyone to have faith and turn toward the Buddha-dharma."
Those who harbor deviant thoughts shall all have their minds rectified;
those yakṣas who act with self-will shall all cease to be arrogant, and they shall all be made to praise the Buddha and protect the Dharma.
"This is essential; it is what the Buddha has taught.
Then the Four Heavenly Kings recited this mantra:
"Whoever seeks out the faults of others shall all be defeated."
The Buddha said to Maitreya and the Bodhisattva Aniruddha:
"I have practiced the bodhisattva path for incalculable eons; I now entrust you with the Dharma, charging you to ensure that it remains long in the world."
Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Tiwuli Bodhisattva:
"After the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, we shall protect this Dharma, instruct and inform others, and extensively expound its matters."
If in future generations there are bodhisattvas who possess merit and shall obtain this sutra scroll, we shall encourage, assist, and protect them.

If in future generations those who obtain this sutra—whether by writing, reciting, chanting, or reading—attain peace and security, you should know that they are protected by Maitreya and the bodhisattva Aniruddha.
At that time, Māra came into the assembly and addressed the Buddha:
"When the Buddha preaches the Dharma for the sake of the śrāvakas, I feel no fear, nor do I have any anxiety."

"The Buddha has now taught the seal of the bodhisattva, the dwelling in the state of a Tathāgata, that which gradually approaches the bodhisattva path and acts as a protection for all beings; having heard this, I am now filled with sorrow."
It is as if one were old and now utterly exhausted, wishing to collapse to the ground; I pray that the Tathāgata will take pity upon me and have compassion for me. Why is this?
Upon hearing this, he was deeply distressed and filled with great sorrow, saying, "From this day forward, do not speak of this again.
The Buddha said, "Māra, do not weep any longer, nor give way to grief; those who are now your companions are also very numerous."
"Those who have not heard this Dharma are all its companions; those who believe and delight in it are but few.
The Buddha then took some soil and placed it upon his fingernail, saying, "Those who have faith and incline toward this Dharma are as numerous as the soil on my fingernail."
The number of those who do not believe is like the soil of the earth.
As numerous as the particles of that soil, so too are the non-believers all his companions; for this reason, he should rejoice.

When this Dharma was being preached, immeasurable beings throughout all realms of humanity all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Ninety-two thousand bodhisattvas all attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*; eighty-four thousand people all attained the stage of *srotāpanna*; and eight thousand bhikṣus all attained *arhatship*.

At that time, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; its radiance shone everywhere without exception, celestial flowers rained down universally, and lutes, harps, and musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.
Countless hosts of devas in the void all exclaimed:
"Excellent, excellent!
We behold the turning of the Wheel of Dharma once again in Jambudvīpa."

Just as when the Tathāgata turned the wheel of Dharma in the realm of Vārāṇasī, many attained peace and security; yet it does not equal even a fraction of what has been taught here today, which is increased by many times over.
"Whoever upholds, recites, chants, or reads this sutra shall be said to assist in the turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Aniruddha, and Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"What kind of dharma is this?"
"How should one practice?
The Buddha said,
"This is titled 'The Chapter on the Questions of the Dhṛtarāṣṭra Regarding the Pāramitās and the Liberation from All Dharma-Jewels.'"

When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Tiwuli, the community of bhikṣus, the devas, humans, gandharvas, ghosts and spirits, and nāgas were all filled with joy; they came forward, prostrated before the Buddha, and departed.
